prep:bei.tx: From Middle High German bī, from Old High German bī, from Proto-West Germanic *bī, from Proto-Germanic *bi. More at by.

verb:befallen.tx: From Middle High German bevallen, from Old High German bifallan, from Proto-West Germanic *bifallan, from Proto-Germanic *bifallaną. Equivalent to be- + fallen. Cognate with Dutch bevallen, English befall.

verb:bitten.tx: From Middle High German bitten, from Old High German bitten, from Proto-West Germanic *biddjan, from Proto-Germanic *bidjaną. Compare Low German bidden, Dutch bidden, English bid, Danish bede.

adj:blond.tx: Borrowed from French blond, from Frankish *blund, from Proto-Germanic *blundaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlendʰ-. The earlier borrowing Middle High German blunt was rare and had no continuation in early modern German.

adj:bourgeois.tx: Borrowed from French bourgeois, name for a wealthy class of French citizens in the late 18th century.

adj:bitter.tx: From Middle High German bitter, pitter, from Old High German bittar, from Proto-West Germanic *bitr.

adv:bitter.tx: From Middle High German bitter, pitter, from Old High German bittar, from Proto-West Germanic *bitr.

adv:bass.tx: From Middle High German baȥ, from Old High German baȥ, from Proto-Germanic *batiz (“better”, adverb), comparative of *wela (“well”), whence German wohl. Represents the old adverb form of besser, whose adverbial use developed in Middle High German. Attributive use of bass, in turn, is much more recent and has remained rare.

adj:bass.tx: From Middle High German baȥ, from Old High German baȥ, from Proto-Germanic *batiz (“better”, adverb), comparative of *wela (“well”), whence German wohl. Represents the old adverb form of besser, whose adverbial use developed in Middle High German. Attributive use of bass, in turn, is much more recent and has remained rare.

noun:Buch.tx: From Middle High German buoch, from Old High German buoh, from Proto-West Germanic *bōk, from Proto-Germanic *bōks. Cognate with English book.

intj:baba.tx: A link of the term with the English bye-bye is possible but not certain.

adj:bang.tx: Originally an adverb, cf. mir ist bange. From Middle High German bange, an enlargement (with the prefix be-) of ange, Old High German ango (“narrowly, anxiously”), an adverb of engi (“narrow”), from Proto-Germanic *anguz.

adj:banal.tx: Borrowed from French banal, from Medieval Latin bannalis, from bannum.

adj:bar.tx: From Middle High German bar, from Old High German bar, from Proto-West Germanic *baʀ, from Proto-Germanic *bazaz (“bare, naked”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰosós, from *bʰos- (“bare, barefoot”). Hence the meanings "without something" (as in bar jeder Einsicht "from every point of view") and "evident to the naked eye" (attested in Middle High German bar in reference to money).

adv:bar.tx: From Middle High German bar, from Old High German bar, from Proto-West Germanic *baʀ, from Proto-Germanic *bazaz (“bare, naked”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰosós, from *bʰos- (“bare, barefoot”). Hence the meanings "without something" (as in bar jeder Einsicht "from every point of view") and "evident to the naked eye" (attested in Middle High German bar in reference to money).

prep:bar.tx: From Middle High German bar, from Old High German bar, from Proto-West Germanic *baʀ, from Proto-Germanic *bazaz (“bare, naked”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰosós, from *bʰos- (“bare, barefoot”). Hence the meanings "without something" (as in bar jeder Einsicht "from every point of view") and "evident to the naked eye" (attested in Middle High German bar in reference to money).

adv:bald.tx: From Middle High German balde, from Old High German baldo, adverb of bald, pald, from Proto-West Germanic *balþ, from Proto-Germanic *balþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-. Cognate with Dutch boud, English bold.

verb:biegen.tx: From Middle High German biegen, from Old High German biogan, from Proto-West Germanic *beugan, from Proto-Germanic *beuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewgʰ- (“to bend”).

noun:Brustwarze.tx: From Brust (“breast”) + Warze (“wart”). Compare Swedish bröstvårta.

adj:breit.tx: From Middle High German breit, from Old High German breit, from Proto-West Germanic *braid, from Proto-Germanic *braidaz.

verb:bergen.tx: From Middle High German bërgen, from Old High German bergan, from Proto-West Germanic *bergan, from Proto-Germanic *berganą.

noun:Birne.tx: From Middle High German bire, bir, from Old High German bira, pira, from Vulgar Latin pira, reanalysis of the plural of Latin pirum. Early Modern German birn is from the Middle High German plural and dative/genitive singular, whence a double plural birnen was formed. The contemporary Birne is a new backformation from this plural (perhaps influenced also by the older, still dialectal form bire). …

adj:böse.tx: From Middle High German bœse, bōse, from Old High German bōsi, from Proto-West Germanic *bausī, from Proto-Germanic *bausuz (“inflated, puffed up, arrogant, bad”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew-, *bew- (“to blow, inflate, swell”), akin to Yiddish בייז (beyz), Dutch boos, and English boast.

adv:böse.tx: From Middle High German bœse, bōse, from Old High German bōsi, from Proto-West Germanic *bausī, from Proto-Germanic *bausuz (“inflated, puffed up, arrogant, bad”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew-, *bew- (“to blow, inflate, swell”), akin to Yiddish בייז (beyz), Dutch boos, and English boast.

verb:baden.tx: From Middle High German baden, from Old High German badōn.

noun:Büffel.tx: From Middle High German büffel, püffel (14th c.), from Middle French bufle, from Italian bufalo, from Late Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos), a derivative of βοῦς (boûs, “ox”).

noun:Bube.tx: From Middle High German buobe (“knave”), from Old High German Buobo, a male name of unknown meaning, though probably formed as a reduplication of a syllable *bo which may be abstracted from Proto-Germanic *brōþēr (“brother”), based on the original meaning of "male child", reinforced by sound-symbolism. Cognate with Dutch boef (“villain”). Probably also related to boy; see there for more.

adj:blad.tx: Borrowed from Bavarian blad (literally “blown up”). Doublet of gebläht.

noun:Bache.tx: From Late Middle High German bache f (“fattened sow, female porker”), by gender change from the word in etymology 2 below; see Bachen. The sense developed from “bacon” via “slaughtered pig” to “porker”. The modern use is from hunters’ jargon.

verb:backen.tx: From Middle High German backen, from Old High German backan, an originally weak verb and geminated variant of an older strong verb: Middle High German bachen, from Old High German bahhan, from Proto-West Germanic *bakan. The two verbs early on were blended to some degree, each developing both weak and strong forms. Bachen was originally the predominant form in Upper German. Backen prevailed in …

noun:Bann.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German ban, from the root of bannen (“to outlaw, banish”).

verb:beschlagen.tx: From Middle High German beslahen, from Old High German bislahan, from Proto-West Germanic *bislahan. Equivalent to be- + schlagen. Cognate with Dutch beslaan.

adj:beschlagen.tx: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

noun:Besuch.tx: From Middle High German besuoch (“test; interest (of borrowed money); right to use a place as pasture grounds”), from Old High German besuoch (“temptation”). Compare German Low German Besök/Besöök, Beseik. By surface analysis, be- + suchen.

adj:blau.tx: From Middle High German blā (genitive blāwes), from Old High German blāo, from Proto-West Germanic *blāu, from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz.

adj:bloß.tx: From Middle High German blōȥ, from Old High German blōȥ (“bare, naked”), from Proto-West Germanic *blaut, from Proto-Germanic *blautaz (“void, emaciated, soft”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlaw- (“weak, frightened”). Cognate with Dutch bloot (“bare, naked”), Danish blød (“soft, weak”), Danish blot (“merely, just”), Swedish blott (“merely, just”), French blouse. More at blouse.

adv:bloß.tx: From Middle High German blōȥ, from Old High German blōȥ (“bare, naked”), from Proto-West Germanic *blaut, from Proto-Germanic *blautaz (“void, emaciated, soft”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlaw- (“weak, frightened”). Cognate with Dutch bloot (“bare, naked”), Danish blød (“soft, weak”), Danish blot (“merely, just”), Swedish blott (“merely, just”), French blouse. More at blouse.

noun:Boden.tx: From Middle High German boden, bodem, from Old High German bodam, from Proto-West Germanic *bodm, from Proto-Germanic *budm-, a variant of *butmaz (whence English bottom, which see for more), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn. Cognate with English bottom, Dutch bodem, Hunsrik Boddem. Doublet of Bodden, a loanword from Low German.

noun:Bote.tx: From Middle High German bote, from Old High German boto, from Proto-Germanic *budô (“messenger”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ-.

noun:Botschaft.tx: From Middle High German botschaft, boteschaft, from Old High German botoscaft, from Proto-West Germanic *bodaskapi, from Proto-Germanic *budaskapiz. By surface analysis, Bote + -schaft. Cognate with German Low German Böskupp, Dutch boodschap (whence also Afrikaans boodskap and Sranan Tongo boskopu), Swedish budskap, Danish budskab (whence also Norwegian Bokmål budskap), Norwegian Nynorsk bodskap, …

adj:braun.tx: From Middle High German brūn, from Old High German brūn, from Proto-West Germanic *brūn.

noun:Backe.tx: From Middle High German backe, from Old High German backo. Further origin uncertain; note, however, the similarity to Ancient Greek φᾰγεῖν (phăgeîn, “eat”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂g- (“to divide, distribute”) (though the same non-trivial semantic shift occurring in two independent branches is unlikely), as well as Latin bucca.

verb:bringen.tx: From Middle High German bringen, from Old High German bringan, from Proto-West Germanic *bringan, from Proto-Germanic *bringaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrenk-. Compare Hunsrik bringe, Low German brengen, Dutch brengen, Afrikaans bring, English bring, West Frisian bringe, Gothic 𐌱𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌲𐌰𐌽 (briggan).

noun:Brezel.tx: From Middle High German brēzel, from Old High German brezitella, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *brāchiātellus (“small cake”), from Latin bracchiātus (“have branches like arms”), from bracchium (“arm”) + -ātus.

adj:blind.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German blint, from Proto-West Germanic *blind.

adj:bunt.tx: From Middle High German bunt, probably from Latin punctus, whence also English point; this would make it a doublet of Punkt. Dutch bont seems to have somewhat earlier attestations in the relevant sense, but the phonetic form (b- for p- and Dutch -o- for -u-) could hint at Middle High German origin. It is therefore unsettled which of the two borrowed from which.

noun:Baum.tx: From Middle High German boum, from Old High German boum, from Proto-West Germanic *baum, from Proto-Germanic *baumaz. Akin to Dutch boom, Low German Boom, West Frisian beam, English beam.

intj:basta.tx: From Late Middle High German basta (15th c.), from Italian basta.

adj:blank.tx: From Middle High German blanc, from Old High German blanc (“shining, bright”), from Proto-West Germanic *blank. Doublet of Plenk.

adj:brutal.tx: From Latin brutalis, from brutus (“dull, stupid”).

noun:Blatt.tx: From Middle High German blat, plat, from Old High German blat, from Proto-West Germanic *blad (“leaf”), from Proto-Germanic *bladą (“leaf”); akin to Low German Blatt, Dutch blad, English blade, Danish and Swedish blad. Indo-European cognates include Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon), Latin folium.

noun:Blume.tx: From Middle High German bluome m or f, from Old High German bluomo m, bluoma f, from Proto-West Germanic *blōmō (“flower”), which see for cognates. The masculine used to be chiefly Upper German, the feminine chiefly Central German. The latter was later reinforced by Middle Low German blôme (exclusively feminine). Analogy with Blüte and Pflanze may also have contributed.

verb:bestrafen.tx: From Middle High German bestrāfen, equivalent to be- + strafen. Cognate with Middle Low German bestraffen, German Low German bestrafen.

noun:Bedarf.tx: From Low German and Middle Low German bedarf, the present stem of bedörven (“to need”), from Old Saxon bi- + tharvōn (“to need, lack, want”). Morphologically identical to the present singular of Middle High German and German bedürfen.

conj:bis.tx: From Middle High German biz, bit, bitze, from bī (“by”) + ze (“to”). Equivalent to modern bei/be- and zu. Compare German Low German bit (“until”), Saterland Frisian bit (“until”). Compare also English up to.

prep:bis.tx: From Middle High German biz, bit, bitze, from bī (“by”) + ze (“to”). Equivalent to modern bei/be- and zu. Compare German Low German bit (“until”), Saterland Frisian bit (“until”). Compare also English up to.

noun:Baby.tx: Mid-19th-century borrowing from English baby. The use as a term of endearment is a later borrowing from late-20th-century pop culture; it remains far more common in pop music than in real life.

noun:Bach.tx: From Middle High German bach m or f, from Old High German bah, from Proto-West Germanic *baki. Cognate with Dutch beek, English beach and beck. The Middle High German gender was chiefly masculine in Upper German, chiefly feminine in Central German. This is one of the rarer cases in which northern gender usage did not establish itself; perhaps because the masculine agrees with the semantically related Fluss and Strom.

noun:Bachelor.tx: Borrowed from English bachelor. Doublet of Bakkalaureus.

noun:Bad.tx: From Middle High German bat, from Old High German bad, from Proto-West Germanic *baþ, from Proto-Germanic *baþą. Related to bähen.

noun:Bagel.tx: A borrowing from English bagel, from Yiddish בייגל (beygl). Doublet of Beugel.

noun:Ball.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German bal, from Proto-West Germanic *ballu, from Proto-Germanic *balluz. Cognates include English ball, Dutch bal, Danish bold, Swedish boll, Icelandic böllur, and Norwegian ball.

noun:Ballast.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German ballast, a compound word the second part of which is Last. The origin of the first part is uncertain; several theories and possible paths of borrowing are discussed.

noun:Banane.tx: 16th century, from Portuguese banana, from a Niger-Congo language of West Africa. A further origin from Arabic بَنان (banān, “fingertips”) has been considered, but there is no particular reason to believe the similarity to be anything but coincidental. (The use of بنان for “banana” in Maghrebi Arabic dialects is borrowed from European languages.) The German form in -e is attested from the 19th …

noun:Band.tx: From Middle High German bant, from Old High German bant, from Proto-West Germanic *band n or m, from Proto-Germanic *bandą ~ *bandaz (“band, bond”), derived from *bindaną (“to bind”). The noun was neuter in most of High German, but masculine in Low German (see Middle Low German bant m) and parts of West Central German. The lexicalisation of this northern usage in the sense “volume” dates from the 17th century.

noun:Bank.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German banc, bank (“height”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz. Related to Old Saxon bank.

noun:Bar.tx: Borrowed in the 19th century from English bar, from Old French barre.

noun:Bark.tx: From Dutch or English bark, both from Old French barque. Doublet of Barke.

noun:Baron.tx: Ca. 1600, from French baron, from Old French baron.

noun:Barren.tx: From Middle High German barre, from Old French barre.

noun:Base.tx: From Middle High German base, from Old High German basa, from Proto-West Germanic *baswā, from Proto-Germanic *baswǭ (“father's sister; paternal aunt”). Compare Saterland Frisian Bääsje (“grandmother”), Dutch baas (“master; boss”). More at boss.

noun:Basilisk.tx: From Middle High German basiliske, from Medieval Latin basiliscus.

noun:Basis.tx: From Middle High German basis (13th c.), from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis). At first in various technical senses. The generalization as “foundation” likely influenced by French base, the military use probably after English base, both from the same Latin noun.

noun:Bass.tx: Borrowed from Italian basso (“low”), from Latin bassus (“low”).

noun:Bast.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German bast (“inner bark of trees”), probably related to besten (“to strap”), from Proto-West Germanic *bastijan (“to plait, sew, weave”).

noun:Bastard.tx: From Middle High German bastart, basthart (“illegitimate child of a nobleman”), from Old French bastart, probably from Frankish, but the precise derivation is uncertain.

noun:Be.tx: Name of the letter B, from its shape.

noun:Beamer.tx: From beamen (“to beam; to project”) + -er; the former from English beam (“to transmit matter or information via a high-tech wireless mechanism”). Inasmuch as the English verb does not share the figurative sense “to project”, the German is a pseudo-anglicism. Compare the same in Dutch beamer (“video projector”).

noun:Beck.tx: From Middle High German becke, from Old High German becko, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz (“baker”). Doublet of Bäcker.

noun:Beet.tx: From Middle High German bette, bete, bet, from Old High German betti, beti (“bed, flower-bed”), from Proto-West Germanic *badi, from Proto-Germanic *badją. Doublet of Bett (“bed for sleeping”). The West Germanic noun had simple -d- in the nominative/accusative and geminated -dd- in the oblique cases. This alternation was generally levelled towards the geminate, but variants with a simple …

noun:Berg.tx: From Middle High German bërc, from Old High German bërg, itself from Proto-West Germanic *berg, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bergaz. Compare Dutch berg, German Low German Barg, Berg, Biärg, West Frisian berch, English berry, barrow, Danish bjerg, Swedish berg.

noun:Beryllium.tx: Beryll + Latin -ium, first used by Friedrich Wöhler in 1828.

noun:Besetzung.tx: From besetzen (“to place, fill, occupy”) + -ung. Compare Dutch bezetting (“occupation”).

noun:Bier.tx: From Middle High German bier, from Old High German bior, from Proto-West Germanic *beuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *beuzą (“beer”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰews-, *bheus- (“dross, sediment, brewer's yeast”). Akin to Dutch bier, Low German Beer, bêr, English beer, Icelandic bjór. More at beer.

noun:Bild.tx: From Middle High German bilde, from Old High German bilidi, biladi, from Proto-West Germanic *biliþi.

noun:Bio.tx: Clipping of biologisch or terms like Biolebensmittel/Bio-Lebensmittel, Biogemüse/Bio-Gemüse.

noun:Bitte.tx: Alteration (after the verb bitten) of obsolete Bete, from Middle High German bete, from Old High German beta, from Proto-Germanic *bedō. Doublet of Bede. Cognate with Dutch bede.

noun:Blase.tx: From Middle High German blāse, from Old High German blāsa, from the root of blasen (“to blow”).

noun:Blitz.tx: From Middle High German blitze (“lightning”), from Old High German blëcchazzen; compare English bleak and bleach. Synchronically analyzed as a nominal formation from blitzen (“to flash”), see there for more. Cognates See also Old Saxon bliksmo (“lightning”), Old English blæcern (“candlestick”), Dutch bliksem, Ancient Greek φλέγω (phlégō, “to burn, blaze”), Sanskrit भ्राज (bhrāja, “to radiate, …

noun:Blitzkrieg.tx: From Blitz (“lightning”) + Krieg (“war”), coined in the runup to the Second World War to denote the "lightning fast" military campaigns planned by the German forces.

noun:Block.tx: From Middle High German bloc, from Old High German bloc. The more common Middle High German form was originally bloch, from Old High German bloh. The variant prevailed in modern German under the reinforcing influence of Middle Low German block. All from Proto-West Germanic *blokk, from Proto-Germanic *blukką. The architectural sense is loaned from English block (and may therefore take a plural in -s).

noun:Blut.tx: From Middle High German bluot, from Old High German bluot, from Proto-West Germanic *blōd, from Proto-Germanic *blōþą, of uncertain origin. Cognates include Bavarian Bluat, Low German Bloot, Dutch bloed, English blood, Danish and Swedish blod and Gothic 𐌱𐌻𐍉𐌸 (blōþ).

noun:Bock.tx: From Middle High German bok, from Old High German bok, from Proto-West Germanic *bukk. Cognate with Dutch bok, English buck, Danish buk, Swedish bock, etc.

noun:Bogen.tx: From Middle High German boge, from Old High German bogo, from Proto-West Germanic *bogō, from Proto-Germanic *bugô. Compare Dutch boog, English bow, Danish bue, Norwegian Nynorsk boge, Swedish båge.

noun:Bonus.tx: Borrowed from English bonus, from Latin.

noun:Boot.tx: Via Middle Low German bōt, from Middle English bot (compare modern English boat).

noun:Bord.tx: From Middle High German bort (inflected bortes), from Old High German bort (“edge, rim”), from Proto-West Germanic *bord. The modern form in -d and the sense “shelf” are due to influence of cognate Middle Low German bort (inflected bordes), from Old Saxon bord. The shifted t remains in related Borte (“border, e.g. on a garment”).

noun:Borg.tx: From Middle High German barc, from Old High German barug, from Proto-West Germanic *barug. The contemporary vocalism is based on Middle Low German borch, which may be an old variant with zero-grade (compare Old English borg). Cognate with Dutch barg, English barrow.

noun:Born.tx: Low and Central German form of Brunnen with r-metathesis. From northern Middle High German born and Middle Low German born(e). See the same in Bernstein, bersten.

noun:Boson.tx: From English boson, from Bose + -on. Named after Indian Bengali physicist and polymath Satyendra Nath Bose; coined by British theoretical physicist Paul Dirac in a lecture titled "Developments in Atomic Theory".

noun:Box.tx: Borrowed from English box. Doublet of Büchse (“can”) and Buchse (“bushing, connector”).

noun:Brand.tx: From Middle High German brant, from Old High German brant, from Proto-West Germanic *brand. Cognate with Bavarian Brånd and English brand. The retention of /d/ in the combination /nd/ is a signature of northern High German dialects and only becomes widespread after a period in the Middle Ages where the southern reflex /nt/ is favoured in southern writings.

noun:Brandy.tx: Borrowed from English brandy, shortened form of brandywine.

noun:Bratwurst.tx: From Middle High German brātwurst, from Old High German brātwurst. The term originally denoted a sausage (Wurst) made of Brät (Old High German brāto), but has come to be used for a sausage that is fried or is suited to being fried (braten). Kluge suggests the modern word might be a conflation of those two etymologies rather than a derivation of only the first one.

noun:Brett.tx: From Middle High German brët, from Old High German brët, from Proto-West Germanic *bred, from Proto-Germanic *bredą, an e-grade byform of *burdą (“board, plank”). Cognate with Old English bred and Yiddish ברעט (bret).

noun:Brief.tx: From Middle High German brief, from Old High German briaf, which is borrowed from Latin breve, a neuter form of brevis (“short”). Cognates include Middle Dutch brief, Dutch brief, Old Norse bréf, Old Saxon brēf (all of them borrowed from Latin) and English brief.

noun:Budget.tx: Borrowed from French budget, from English budget.

noun:Buffet.tx: Borrowed from French buffet. The spelling Büfett, preferred at least in Germany, represents the Germanised pronunciation in /ɛt/. Such a pronunciation has established itself in many words like Parkett, Kabarett, etc. In the case of Buffet, however, the French pronunciation has widely prevailed, which means that speakers now often pronounce /eː/ while reading and writing Büfett.

noun:Bug.tx: From Middle High German buoc (“animal shoulder”), from Old High German buog (“animal shoulder”), from Proto-West Germanic *bōgu, from Proto-Germanic *bōguz (“arm; shoulder”). More at English bough. The common contemporary meaning “bow” (early 17th c.) is a semantic loan from Middle Low German bôch, from Old Saxon bōg, from the same Germanic noun.

noun:Bund.tx: Inherited from Middle High German bunt, ultimately equivalent to a deverbal of binden (“bind”).

noun:Bungalow.tx: Borrowed from English bungalow, from Hindi बंगला (baṅglā).

noun:Burger.tx: Borrowed from English burger, from hamburger, from German Hamburger (“of the city Hamburg”).

noun:Burka.tx: Borrowed from Urdu; see burka for more.

noun:Burke.tx: From Baltic German, from Swedish burk.

noun:Butter.tx: From Middle High German buter, butter, from Old High German butera, from Proto-West Germanic *buterā (“butter”). Though originally feminine, the word became masculine throughout Upper German and in southern dialects of West Central German. The now established feminine gender is East Central German, reinforced by Middle Low German boter f.

noun:Bär.tx: From Middle High German bër m, Old High German bëro m, from Proto-West Germanic *berō, from Proto-Germanic *berô, conventionally taken to be a taboo-avoidance term derived from the word for "brown". Compare Dutch beer, English bear, West Frisian bear, Danish bjørn.

noun:Böse.tx: From Middle High German bōse, from Old High German bōsi. Cognate with English boast.

noun:Boutique.tx: In the archaic sense (15th c.) from Middle French boutique. The contemporary sense is a 20th-century semantic loan from Modern French boutique (due to the prestige of French in the world of fashion). Doublet of Apotheke, Bodega, and Bottich.

noun:Bison.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin bisōn, bisōnt-, at first also in forms with -t such as Bisont. Perhaps reinforced by French bison of the same source. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wisundaz and thus a doublet of Wisent.

noun:Bühne.tx: From Middle High German büne (“wooden stage, platform, deck, ceiling”), see there for more.

noun:Bürste.tx: From Middle High German bürste, plural (and dative/genitive singular) of burst, from Old High German *burst (“bristle”, attested as plural burste, pursti), from Proto-West Germanic *bursti, from Proto-Germanic *burstiz. Compare related Borste (“bristle”).

verb:bürsten.tx: From Middle High German bürsten; see Borste (“brush, bristle”).

noun:Bahn.tx: From Middle High German ban, from Old High German *bana, from Proto-West Germanic *banu, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *banō. Cognate with Luxembourgish Bunn, Dutch baan.

noun:Bauernhof.tx: From compound Bauer (“farmer”) + -n- + Hof (“yard; enclosure”). Akin to Dutch boerenhof.

noun:Bauer.tx: From Middle High German būre, gebūre, from Old High German būr (“peasant”), gibūr, gibūro. All these forms ultimately descend from Proto-West Germanic *būr, itself from Proto-Germanic *būraz (“inhabitant, dweller”). Compare English boor.

verb:bauen.tx: From Middle High German būwen, from Old High German būan, from Proto-West Germanic *būan, from Proto-Germanic *būaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰúHt, the athematic root aorist of the root *bʰuH-.

verb:bahnen.tx: From Middle High German banen. Equivalent to Bahn (“trail, route”) + -en.

noun:Bus.tx: From Omnibus, with influence from English bus.

noun:Brot.tx: From Middle High German brōt, from Old High German brōt (attested since the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *braud, from Proto-Germanic *braudą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrew- (“to seethe, to boil”). Originally, the meaning of Brot was "what has been fermented, leaven" and may be a nominal derivative from Proto-Germanic *brewwaną (“to brew”) (whence German brauen). It replaced the older …

noun:Bulette.tx: Borrowed from French boulette de viande (“small ball of beef”).

noun:Bulle.tx: Via German Low German from Middle Low German bulle. Cognate with Dutch bul. More at bull.

noun:Blei.tx: From Middle High German blī, from Old High German blīo, from Proto-West Germanic *blīwī.

verb:bescheißen.tx: From Middle High German beschīȥen, from Old High German biskīȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *biskītan, equivalent to be- + scheißen. Cognate with German Low German beschieten, Dutch beschijten, English beshite.

verb:beißen.tx: From Middle High German bīȥen, from Old High German bīȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *bītan, from Proto-Germanic *bītaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéydt (“to split”). Cognate with Dutch bijten, Low German bieten, English bite, Danish bide, Swedish bita.

noun:Bett.tx: From Middle High German bet, bette, from Old High German betti, from Proto-West Germanic *badi, from Proto-Germanic *badją (“plot, grave, resting-place, bed”). Cognate with Low German Bedd, Dutch bed, West Frisian bêd, English bed, Swedish bädd, Icelandic beður. Doublet of Beet.

verb:behandeln.tx: From Middle High German behandeln (“to touch with the hand”), equivalent to be- + handeln. Compare Saterland Frisian behondelje, Dutch behandelen, English behandle.

verb:belassen.tx: From Middle High German belâzen, from Old High German bilâzan. Equivalent to be- + lassen.

verb:bekommen.tx: From Middle High German bekomen, from Old High German biquëman, bikwëman, from Proto-West Germanic *bikweman, from Proto-Germanic *bikwemaną, equivalent to be- + kommen. Cognate to Dutch bekomen, English become.

verb:basteln.tx: An Upper German verb, from earlier besteln, iterative of Middle High German besten, from Proto-West Germanic *bastijan. The -a- is perhaps dialectal or through readaptation to the underlying noun Bast (“bast”).

verb:beginnen.tx: From Middle High German beginnen, from Old High German biginnan, from Proto-West Germanic *biginnan, from Proto-Germanic *biginnaną. Cognate with Low German beginnen, Dutch beginnen, West Frisian begjinne, and English begin.

verb:bestellen.tx: From Middle High German bestellen, from Old High German bistellen. Equivalent to be- + stellen.

noun:Bauch.tx: From Middle High German būch, from Old High German būh, from Proto-Germanic *būkaz (“belly, body”). More at bouk.

noun:Bahre.tx: From Middle High German bāre, from Old High German bāra, from Proto-West Germanic *bāru, from Proto-Germanic *bērō.

verb:beten.tx: From Middle High German beten, from Old High German betōn.

noun:Bure.tx: Backformation of Dutch Boeren, plural of Boer. The word originally means “farmer” in Dutch but also in several German dialects, which is probably why the form Bur was avoided in German. (The word Bauer, and even more Bur as a dialectal form, may have the pejorative implication of an illiterate person. Compare English boor.)

noun:Brut.tx: From Middle High German pruot, bruot, from Old High German pruot, bruot, from Proto-Germanic *brōduz (“warmth; brood”).

noun:Barsch.tx: From Middle High German bars, from Old High German bars, from Proto-West Germanic *bars. Cognate with Dutch baars, English bass (earlier barse).

noun:Bockbier.tx: From Bock (“beer from Einbeck”) + Bier, see the former for more.

noun:Bohne.tx: From Middle High German bone, from Old High German bōna, from Proto-West Germanic *baunu, from Proto-Germanic *baunō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ- (“bean”). Compare Danish bønne, Dutch boon, English bean, Low German Bohn, West Frisian bean.

noun:Biene.tx: From Middle High German bine, from Old High German bini, from Proto-West Germanic *bini.

noun:Baldachin.tx: From Middle High German baldekīn, from Italian baldacchino, derived from Baldacca (“the city of Baghdad”), from Arabic بَغْداد (baḡdād), from Middle Persian. The modern German spelling and pronunciation through readaptation to the Italian form, likely reinforced by association with Dach (“roof”).

noun:Beere.tx: From Middle High German ber, bere n (sometimes f), from Old High German beri n, from Proto-Germanic *bazją n. Cognate with English berry and eventually Dutch bes. Chiefly in Upper German, the final vowel was lost through early apocope after short vowel + single sonorant. The -e was maintained in the north, however, where it led to a shift to the feminine gender (compare Middle Low German bēre f), …

noun:Brombeere.tx: With dialectal -ā- → -ō- and subsequent shortening from Middle High German brāmber, from Old High German brāmberi, from Proto-West Germanic *brāmabaʀi (“blackberry, bramble”). Compare Dutch braambes, English bramberry, French framboise.

noun:Bisam.tx: From Middle High German bisem, from Old High German bisam, bisamo, borrowed from Medieval Latin bisamum, from Hebrew בֹּשֶׂם (bāśām, bōśem, “perfume”). Doublet of Balsam (“balm, balsam”) and Desman.

noun:Beschilderung.tx: From beschildern + -ung, further from be- + Schilder + -ung.

noun:Beutel.tx: From Middle High German biutel, from Old High German būtil, from Proto-West Germanic *būdil (“bag, purse”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to blow, swell”). Cognate with Dutch buidel, Yiddish בײַטלען (baytlen).

noun:Binde.tx: From Middle High German binde, from Old High German binta, from the root of binden (“to bind”).

noun:Bambus.tx: From early modern Dutch bamboes (contemporary bamboe), from Portuguese bambus, plural of bambu, from Malay bambu, from Kannada ಬಂಬು (bambu).

noun:Brust.tx: From Middle High German brust, from Old High German brust, from Proto-West Germanic *brust, from Proto-Germanic *brusts.

noun:Bart.tx: Inherited from Middle High German bart, from Old High German bart, from Proto-West Germanic *bard, from Proto-Germanic *bardaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰéh₂ (“beard”), possibly from *bʰers-. Compare Dutch baard, Luxembourgish Baart, West Frisian burd, English beard.

noun:Bücherei.tx: A calque of Latin librāria, possibly through Dutch boekerij, which seems to be slightly older. Analyzable as Bücher (“books”) + -ei or Buch (“book”) + -erei, ultimately translatable as "bookery".

noun:Bibliothek.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin bibliothēca, from Ancient Greek βῐβλῐοθήκη (bĭblĭothḗkē).

noun:Bibel.tx: From Middle High German bibel, biblie, ultimately from Ancient Greek βιβλία (biblía, “books”). Doublet of Fibel.

noun:Blech.tx: From Middle High German blëch, from Old High German blëh, from Proto-West Germanic *blik, from Proto-Germanic *bliką. Compare Old Saxon blek, Dutch blik.

noun:Backbord.tx: From Middle Low German backbort, bakbort (15th c.). Compare Dutch bakboord (1599), Old English bæcbord (ca. 885).

noun:Burg.tx: From Middle High German burc, from Old High German burg, from Proto-West Germanic *burg, from Proto-Germanic *burgz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰérǵʰ-s, a form of Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“fortified elevation”). Compare Dutch burcht, English borough, ‑bury, Danish borg.

noun:Baptist.tx: Borrowed from Latin baptista, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστής (baptistḗs).

noun:Blick.tx: From Middle High German blic, from Old High German blik, from Proto-Germanic *blikaz, *blikkaz (“shine, appearance, look; metal”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyǵ- (“to shine”). Cognate with Dutch blik (“look, glance”), Danish blik (“look, glance; tin”), Icelandic blik (“gleam, shine”), Old English blice (“an exposure, manifestation”). More at blick.

verb:buchen.tx: From Buch + -en, probably modelled after English to book.

verb:beschränken.tx: From Middle High German beschrenken, from Old High German biskrenken. Equivalent to be- + schränken.

verb:binden.tx: From Middle High German binden, from Old High German bintan, from Proto-West Germanic *bindan, from Proto-Germanic *bindaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ-. Cognate with Low German binnen, binden, Dutch binden, English bind, Danish binde.

verb:bleiben.tx: From Middle High German blīben, belīben (“to remain in the same position, pause, blin”), from Old High German bilīban (“to remain”), from Proto-Germanic *bilībaną (“to remain”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick, glue”). Cognate with Dutch blijven (“to remain”), English belive (“to remain, stay”). More at belive.

noun:Bereich.tx: From the obsolete verb bereichen (“to extend; to cover”, literally “bereach”).

adj:baff.tx: From an interjection for “bang, boom”, now usually in the form paff, of onomatopoeic origin.

verb:branden.tx: Originally to "move like flames," "blaze," from Brand (“blaze, fire”).

verb:bewegen.tx: From Middle High German bewëgen, from Old High German biwëgan, from Proto-West Germanic *biwegan, derived from Proto-Germanic *weganą (“to move”), which stems from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-. Compare English beweigh.

verb:bellen.tx: From Middle High German bëllen, from Old High German bëllan, from Proto-Germanic *bellaną, cognate with English bellow, Russian блеять (blejatʹ, “baa", "bleat”).

prep:binnen.tx: From Middle Low German binnen (“within”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bi- (“by, at”) + *innan << *in (“in”). The form is also Central German in Middle High German binnen (compare Luxembourgish bannen). It is originally an adverb meaning “within, inside” chiefly in local sense, equivalent to German innen. Binnen was adopted in modern standard German as a temporal preposition, while the prefix …

det:beide.tx: From Middle High German beide, bēde, from Old High German beide, bēde, from Proto-Germanic *bai.

pron:beide.tx: From Middle High German beide, bēde, from Old High German beide, bēde, from Proto-Germanic *bai.

noun:Buchstabe.tx: From Middle High German buochstabe, from Old High German *buohstabo (“letter, writing”) (attested only as Old High German buohstab; > German Buchstab), from Proto-West Germanic *bōkstabō, from Proto-Germanic *bōkstabô, a variant of *bōkstabaz. Compare English bookstaff, bookstave.

noun:Bruder.tx: From Middle High German bruoder, from Old High German bruoder, from Proto-West Germanic *brōþer, from Proto-Germanic *brōþēr, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr. Doublet of Frater.

noun:Berber.tx: Borrowed from French berbère, from Arabic بَرْبَر (barbar), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “non-Greek”). Doublet of Barbar.

noun:Becher.tx: From Middle High German bëcher, from Old High German bëhhâri, from Proto-West Germanic *bikārī. Displaced native Stauf in Early New High German. Cognate with English beaker.

adj:brach.tx: Backformation from brachliegen, from in Brache liegen, from the noun Brache (“fallow land, fallowness”). Cognate with Dutch braak. Related with brechen (etymology 2).

verb:bieten.tx: From Middle High German bieten, from Old High German biotan, from Proto-West Germanic *beudan, from Proto-Germanic *beudaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“be awake, aware”). Compare Low German bieden, beden, Dutch bieden, English bid, bede, Danish byde, Swedish bjuda.

verb:brechen.tx: From Middle High German brëchen, from Old High German brëhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *brekan, from Proto-Germanic *brekaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg-. Akin to Old Saxon brekan, Dutch breken (“to break”), English break.

noun:Bolzen.tx: From Middle High German bolz, from Old High German bolz, from Proto-West Germanic *bolt. Compare Dutch bout, English bolt, Danish bolt, Icelandic bolti.

noun:Brücke.tx: From Middle High German brucke, from Old High German brugga, brucca, from Proto-West Germanic *bruggju. The neurological sense “pons” is a semantic loan from Latin pōns. Cognates Compare Bavarian Bruckn, Dutch brug, English bridge, Low German Brügg, Danish brygge, Old Saxon bruggia.

noun:Braten.tx: From Middle High German brate, from Old High German brāto, from Proto-Germanic *brēdô.

noun:Buche.tx: From Middle High German buoche, from Old High German buohha, from Proto-West Germanic *bōku and *bōkijā (both “beech”). The first West Germanic form corresponds to Old English bōc, Old Frisian bōk, the second to Old English bēċe (English beech), Dutch beuk, Luxembourgish Bich. The Standard German form can continue either variant, in the first case regularly, in the second with Upper German umlaut …

noun:Bruch.tx: From Middle High German bruch, from Old High German bruh, from Proto-West Germanic *bruki. Cognate with English breach.

noun:Braut.tx: From Middle High German brūt, from Old High German brūt (akin to Old Saxon brūd), from Proto-West Germanic *brūdi, from Proto-Germanic *brūdiz. Compare Dutch bruid, English bride, Danish brud.

adj:bereit.tx: From Middle High German bereite, from Old High German bireiti, reiti; from Proto-West Germanic *raidī, from the Proto-Germanic base *raidaz (“ready”). Cognate with English ready, Vilamovian byrat.

noun:Buße.tx: From Middle High German buoze, from Old High German buoza, from Proto-West Germanic *bōtu, akin to Old Saxon bōta and Dutch boete. More at English bote, boot.

adj:brut.tx: Borrowed from French brut, from Latin brūtus.

noun:Bäcker.tx: From northern Middle High German becker, from Old High German beckeri, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz. By surface analysis, backen + -er. Upper German originally used the words Beck and Pfister instead. The Central German form was reinforced by Middle Low German becker, from Old Saxon backeri. Both possibly from Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz (compare also Dutch bakker, English baker).

verb:betreiben.tx: From be- + treiben. A calque of Middle Low German bedrīven.

noun:Bürger.tx: From Middle High German burger, burgære, from Old High German burgāri. By surface analysis, Burg + -er.

noun:Brache.tx: From Middle High German brāche, from Old High German brāhha, from Proto-West Germanic *brāku. Cognate with Luxembourgish Brooch, Dutch braak. Related with brechen (“to break”), so called because the field is ploughed (“broken”) and then left in this state.

noun:Brille.tx: From Middle High German brille, berille, from berillus (“beryl”), from Latin beryllus (“beryl”). Compare dialectal English brills (“spectacles”). The "toilet seat" sense is derived in analogy with the usually round shape of spectacle frames surrounding the glass, just as a toilet seat surrounds the toilet hole.

verb:blasen.tx: From Middle High German blāsen, from Old High German blāsan, from Proto-West Germanic *blāsan.

verb:begleiten.tx: From Middle High German begleiten (14th c.), from an underlying (apparently unattested) *begeleiten, a confluence of beleiten and geleiten, both prefixed forms of leiten (“to lead”). Compare Dutch begeleiden. Sometimes reanalyzed as be- + Geleit (“escort”) + -en (with syncope as in begnügen from genug).

noun:Balken.tx: From Middle High German balke, from Old High German balko, balcho, from Proto-West Germanic *balkō, from Proto-Germanic *balkô. Compare English balk.

noun:Buckel.tx: From Middle High German buckel, from Old French boucle, from Latin buccula.

noun:Bernstein.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German bernstein, barnstēn. Pertaining to brennen (“to burn”) with Low German metathesis of -r- (compare bersten, Born). Cognate with English brimstone and Old Norse brennisteinn. The word was borrowed from Middle Low German into several Scandinavian and Slavic languages.

verb:brennen.tx: From Middle High German brennen, a merger of Old High German brennan (from Proto-West Germanic *brannijan), and Old High German brinnan (from *brinnan). Cognate with Bavarian brenna, Dutch branden, Swedish brinna, Icelandic brenna, Old English birnan, and therefore English burn.

noun:Becken.tx: From Middle High German becken, from Old High German becki, beckin, from Vulgar Latin *baccīnum (possibly attested as bacchinon, 6th century), probably from Gaulish. Compare Dutch bekken and further French bassin, English basin.

noun:Biss.tx: From Middle High German biȥ, from Old High German biȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *biti, from Proto-Germanic *bitiz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”). Cognate with Old English bite. In Dutch beet, English bit, this word has been merged with Proto-Germanic *bitô, whence German Bissen. (Modern English bite is a new derivation from the verb.)

noun:Bau.tx: From Middle High German bū, bou, from Old High German bū, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *būą (“building, dwelling”). The plural form Bauten is that of the related Low German Bude (“building”), from Middle Low German bûwete. The singular Baute did not catch on in standard German.

noun:Bausch.tx: From Middle High German būsch, from Old High German būsc; if the original meaning was "cudgel", then perhaps related to bozzan (“to beat”), from Proto-West Germanic *bautan. Related to Beule (“bump, swelling”).

noun:Beginn.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German bigin, from Proto-Germanic *biginnaz (“beginning”), a nominal formation from Proto-Germanic *biginnaną (“to begin”). Cognate with German Low German Begünn.

noun:Beichte.tx: From Middle High German bīht, begiht, from Old High German bigiht, bijiht, from bi- + jiht (“statement, confession”), from Proto-Germanic *jihtiz, equivalent to bei- + Gicht. Cognate with Luxembourgish Beicht, Dutch biecht.

noun:Behörde.tx: Derived from the German Low German and Middle Low German verb behören (“to belong”), for which High German usually uses gehören. The sense is “responsible institution”.

noun:Befehl.tx: From Middle High German *bevël, synchronically analyzed as a deverbal noun from befehlen (“to order, command”). Compare also Dutch bevel.

noun:Beil.tx: From Middle High German bīl, bīhel, from Old High German bīhal (whence also Bavarian Beichl), attested (in the form witubil) since the 8th century, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bīþlą (“axe”), instrumental noun from *bītaną (“to bite”). Compare Dutch bijl. Conflated early on with Proto-Germanic *bilją and its descendants (German Bille). (Kluge mentioned that, in his day, a relationship to Bicke …

noun:Bein.tx: From Middle High German bein, from Old High German bein, from Proto-West Germanic *bain, from Proto-Germanic *bainą. Compare Dutch been, English bone, Danish ben.

noun:Beispiel.tx: From Middle High German bīspil, bīspel, from Old High German bīspel (“proverb", "example”), equivalent to bī- (“by-”) + spel (“talk”), the latter from Proto-Germanic *spellą (“news, message, tale”). Cognate with Old English bīspel (“proverb", "example”), English byspel (“example”). Unrelated to spielen (“to play”).

noun:Bengel.tx: From Middle High German bengel, from Old High German *bengil (“club", "stick", "hammer”), from Proto-West Germanic *bangil, from Proto-Germanic *bangilaz (“club, hammer”), from Proto-Germanic *bang- (“to beat”).

noun:Besen.tx: From Middle High German bëseme, from Old High German bësamo, pësamo (“broom”), from Proto-West Germanic *besmō (“branch, rod, broom”).

noun:Bete.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German bête, from Old Saxon *bēta, from Proto-West Germanic *bētā (“beet”).

noun:Beule.tx: From Middle High German biule, from Old High German būilla, būlla, būla, bulla, from Proto-Germanic *būlijǭ, *būlǭ. Cognate with Dutch buil, English boil.

noun:Beute.tx: From late Middle High German biute, borrowed from Middle Low German büte, whence also the forms in other languages like Dutch buit, English booty, French butin. Of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly a Celtic borrowing, from Proto-Celtic *boudi (“victory, booty, spoils”). If so, related to the name of Boudica, a British Celtic queen.

noun:Biber.tx: From Middle High German biber, from Old High German bibar, bibur, from Proto-West Germanic *bebru, from Proto-Germanic *bebruz (“beaver”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰébʰrus. The spelling with ⟨i⟩ instead of ⟨ie⟩ is unusual. Biber is perhaps the only inherited Germanic word in which /iː/ is spelt ⟨i⟩ without there being a special reason for this (e.g. homophone disambiguation as in Lid, …

noun:Binse.tx: From Middle High German bineʒ, from Old High German binuz, from Proto-West Germanic *binut. The idiom “in die Binsen gehen” is explained from the idea of hunted game being lost when the deer has alighted in the plants. It occurs also with Wicken.

noun:Birke.tx: From Middle High German birke, from Old High German birka, bircha, from Proto-West Germanic *birkijā. The Old High German variant birihha shows a svarabhakti vowel; if continued it would have led to modern *Birche (compare Kirche). Cognate to Dutch berk, Low German Bark, English birch, Swedish björk.

noun:Bischof.tx: From Middle High German bischof, from Old High German biscof, from Proto-West Germanic *biskop, from Latin episcopus. The -f- is due to the High German consonant shift, but in Middle High German it irregularly developed into -v- (thus predominantly bischoves rather than bischoffes), which explains the (variably) lengthened vowel. This development has been ascribed to renewed Romance influence; …

adj:blass.tx: From Middle High German blas, itself from Old High German blas, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *blas.

verb:blenden.tx: From Middle High German blenden, from Old High German blenten, from Proto-Germanic *blandijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlendʰ-. Cognate with Dutch blenden, Old English blendan.

noun:Bohle.tx: 15th century, from Middle High German bole, or from or akin to Middle Low German bōle (“thick board”, 14th c.), probably from Proto-Germanic *bulaz (“trunk; plank”), and ultimately related to Ball (“ball”). Cognate with Middle Dutch bolle, Old Norse bolr (see there for more), English bole (all “tree trunk”), and further with the family of Bolle (“round object”).

noun:Borke.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German borke, from Proto-Germanic *barkuz. Cognate with Dutch and English bark.

noun:Bügel.tx: From Middle High German *bügel (attested as bügele f, later bogell m [15th c.]), from Proto-Germanic *bugilaz, from the root of *beuganą (“to bend, bow”). Cognate with Dutch beugel, Middle Low German bȫgel (earlier already Old Saxon armbugil), Old Norse bygill (whence Danish bøjle etc.). It seems that the word was originally northern (Low and Central German) and established itself more widely …

noun:Bündel.tx: From late Middle High German bündel, diminutive of bunt; equivalent to Bund + -el.

noun:Bürge.tx: From Middle High German bürge, from Old High German burgeo.

noun:Borste.tx: From Middle High German borste, from Old High German borsta, bursta, from Proto-West Germanic *borstā, *burstā, an early stem variant of *bursti, whence German Bürste (“brush”), which compare. Both words originally meant “bristle”, the semantic distinction is a later development. Immediately cognate with Old Saxon bursta (also *borsta as evidenced by Westphalian Boarste, Buoste).

noun:Busch.tx: From Middle High German busch, bosch, from Old High German busk, from Proto-West Germanic *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz. Compare Dutch bos, English bush, Danish busk.

noun:Bursche.tx: From Middle High German burse, from Old High German bursa, from Late Latin bursa.

noun:Bude.tx: From Middle High German buode, from Old High German *buoda, from Proto-West Germanic *bōþu, from Proto-Germanic *bōþō. Probably related to *būaną (“to build”), whence German bauen. Cognate with Middle Dutch boede, Middle Low German bôde, Old Norse búð, bóð, whence English booth.

noun:Busen.tx: From Middle High German buosem, from Old High German buosum, from Proto-Germanic *bōsmaz. Cognate with Dutch boezem, English bosom.

noun:Büchse.tx: Inherited from Middle High German bühse. Doublet of Buchse (the Upper German form).

noun:Bottich.tx: From Middle High German botech, boteche, Old High German botega, potacha (“large barrel”) (9th century). Primarily Upper German, likely loaned from a Late Latin variant of apothēca (“storage room, wine cellar”), in Middle Latin also "barrel, vessel, container", making it a doublet of Apotheke, Bodega, and Boutique, or from Latin butica, Late Latin buttis (“barrel”). The Old High German word was …

noun:Brauch.tx: From Middle High German brūch, from Old High German brūh (“use”, noun), ultimately from the root of brauchen (“to need”).

noun:Braue.tx: From Middle High German brā (inflected brāw-; rarely also brāwe), from Old High German brāwa (late also brā), from Proto-West Germanic *brāwu, from Proto-Germanic *brēwō. Cognate with Dutch brauw, English brow.

noun:Brause.tx: Deverbal from brausen (“to whoosh, to roar”).

noun:Brei.tx: From Middle High German brīe, brī, from Old High German brīo, from Proto-West Germanic *brīw. Cognate with Yiddish ברײַ (bray).

noun:Breite.tx: From Middle High German breite, from Old High German breitī, from Proto-Germanic *braidį̄. Analysable as breit + -e. Compare English breadth.

noun:Bremse.tx: From Middle High German bremse, borrowed from Middle Low German premese (“twitch for horses”), from the verb pramen (“to clamp”), with further origin unclear (DWDS).

noun:Brocken.tx: From Old High German brocco, from Proto-Germanic *brukkô, related to *brukiz.

noun:Brühe.tx: From Middle High German brüeje, from Proto-Germanic *brōaną, whence brauen. Related to brühen.

noun:Brunnen.tx: From Middle High German brunne, from Old High German brunno, from Proto-West Germanic *brunnō, from Proto-Germanic *brunnô, whence also Old English burna, Old Norse brunnr; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrun- (“a bubbling forth; a fountain, wellspring, source”). The form is Upper German, most Low and Central German dialects using Born (now poetic in the standard language). This southern …

noun:Brunst.tx: From Middle High German brunst, from Old High German brunst, from Proto-Germanic *brunstiz.

noun:Bucht.tx: 17th century, from Low German, from Middle Low German bucht, from Old Saxon buht, from Proto-West Germanic *buhti, from Proto-Germanic *buhtiz. Cognate with Dutch bocht, English bight.

noun:Bräune.tx: From Middle High German briune (“brownness”); equivalent to braun + -e (“-ness”).

noun:Bräutigam.tx: From Middle High German briutegome, from Old High German brūtigomo, from Proto-Germanic *brūdigumô (“bride's man”), from *brūdiz (“bride”) + *gumô (“man”). The modern -i- (from Middle High German -e-) is due to palatisation before -g-, which has been pronounced as a fricative in many dialects. The -a- is a northern variant first attested in Middle Low German brǖdegam and northern Middle High …

verb:bilden.tx: From Middle High German bilden, bileden, a merger from Old High German biliden, from Proto-West Germanic *biliþþjan, and Old High German bilidōn, from Proto-West Germanic *biliþōn, both derived from *biliþi (whence German Bild). By surface analysis, Bild + -en. Cognate with Dutch beelden and Swedish bilda.

verb:bombardieren.tx: 17th century, from French bombarder. Equivalent to (archaic) Bombarde + -ieren.

adj:blöd.tx: From Middle High German blode, from Old High German blōdi, from Proto-Germanic *blauþijaz, *blauþaz (“weak, soft, timid”). Cognate with Old English blēaþ (“gentle, shy, cowardly, timid; slothful, inactive, effeminate”), English blate (“bashful, stupid”) and bloat (“be swollen, be worthless”) and Danish blød (“soft”).

verb:beben.tx: From Middle High German biben, from Old High German bibēn, from Proto-West Germanic *bibēn, from Proto-Germanic *bibāną. The modern vocalism is from Middle Low German beven, from Old Saxon bibōn.

verb:bersten.tx: From Middle High German brësten, from Old High German brëstan, from Proto-West Germanic *brestan, from Proto-Germanic *brestaną. The modern form is from Middle Low German with metathesis of -r- from Old Saxon brestan (compare Bernstein, Born). Cognate with Dutch barsten, English burst, Old Norse bresta (whence Danish briste, Norwegian Bokmål briste and Swedish brista).

verb:beugen.tx: From Middle High German böugen, from Old High German bougen, from Proto-Germanic *baugijaną. In early modern German, almost fully merged with related biegen, which used to have the strong 2nd and 3rd persons singular du beugst, er beugt (compare similar archaic forms like du fleugst from fliegen). The later grammarians tried to distinguish the verbs again, though often in ways different from the …

adj:billig.tx: From Middle High German billich, from Old High German billīh (“appropriate”), from Proto-West Germanic *bilalīk.

verb:bohren.tx: From Old High German borōn, from Proto-Germanic *burōną.

verb:borgen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German borgen, from Old High German borgēn, from Proto-West Germanic *borgōn. Cognate with English borrow.

verb:brauen.tx: From Middle High German brūwen, briuwen, from Old High German briuwan. The form shows the Central German development of Middle High German -iuw- → -ūw-, which is only sporadically reflected in the modern standard language (compare kauen).

noun:Beton.tx: Borrowed from French béton (“concrete”), from Latin bitūmen (“asphalt”). Doublet of Bitumen.

verb:batten.tx: Debated. A comparable form is synonymous Dutch baten, which pertains to the Germanic root at hand in English batten and better. At least a secondary relation with this Dutch verb seems certain. However, its regular cognate is Old High German bazzen (“to batten”), which would have led to modern *bassen, bässen. Mere borrowing from Low German or Dutch is unlikely since the verb has -t- in western …

verb:bluten.tx: From Middle High German bluoten, from Old High German bluoten, bluotēn, from Proto-West Germanic *blōdijan.

verb:brauchen.tx: From Middle High German brūchen, from Old High German brūhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *brūkan (“use, employ, consume”). Cognate to English brook and Dutch bruiken.

verb:bezwingen.tx: From Middle High German betwingen, from Old High German bidwingan, from Proto-West Germanic *biþwingan. Equivalent to be- + zwingen.

noun:Blüte.tx: From Middle High German blüete, from older bluot, from Old High German bluot, from Proto-Germanic *blōdiz (“blossom, sprout”). Middle High German bluot was originally a feminine inflecting to blüete in the plural and genitive/dative singular; later this alternation was levelled either by generalizing the form blüete or by converting bluot into a masculine. Related with blühen and Blume. Cognate …

verb:blühen.tx: From Middle High German blüe(je)n, from Old High German bluo(w)en, from Proto-West Germanic *blōan. Cognate with Luxembourgish bléien, Dutch bloeien, English blow.

noun:Bertram.tx: From Middle High German bërtram, bërhtram, from Old High German bërhtram, from Latin pyrethrum and influenced by the male given name, from Ancient Greek πύρεθρον (púrethron).

verb:bedenken.tx: From Middle High German bedenken, from Old High German pidenken, bidenken, bithenken, from Proto-West Germanic *biþankijan, from Proto-Germanic *biþankijaną, equivalent to be- + denken. Cognate with English bethink, Dutch bedenken.

noun:Butt.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Butt, from Middle Low German but, butte, from Old Saxon *butt, from Proto-Germanic *buttaz (“stumpy”). Cognate with Dutch bot and with English butt, in all senses. Apparently this word had the primitive meaning of being a stump, i. e. being flattened by reason of beating, whereby the root might be identified with the one of English beat and German bossen, bosseln.

verb:blinken.tx: From Low German and Middle Low German blinken, ultimately from the root of blecken (“to bare”). Cognate with Dutch blinken.

verb:beleidigen.tx: From Middle High German beleidegen, intensification of leidegen, leidigen, from Old High German leidegōn, leidegen, from leideg, leidig (“hurt, saddened”). Equivalent to be- + leidig + -en.

noun:Büro.tx: Ca. 1700, from French bureau (“desk, office”), which see.

noun:Boxhandschuh.tx: From Boxen (“boxing”) + Hand (“hand”) + Schuh (“shoe”) or boxen + Handschuh.

noun:Batterie.tx: In the military sense (early 17th c.) from French batterie. The electronic sense (late 18th c.) is a semantic loan from English battery.

noun:Begleitung.tx: From begleiten (“to accompany”), or more figuratively, “to walk hand in hand together”. Used by the European Alliance of YMCAs in the context of people development.

noun:Benzin.tx: Coined by German chemist Eilhard Mitscherlich in 1833 from Benzoe + -in.

noun:Brandstifter.tx: 16th century, from Brand (“fire”) + stiften (“to bring about”) + -er (agentive suffix). The formation appears to be of Lower Rhenish origin, being first attested as Ripuarian brant stichter (1507) and Dutch brandtstichter (1542), both with the development ft > cht (as in Nichte etc.).

noun:Brandstiftung.tx: 17th century, from Brand (“fire”) + stiften (“to bring about”) + -ung (“-ing”). Formed after earlier Brandstifter (“arsonist”).

noun:Bergwerk.tx: From Middle High German bercwerc. Equivalent to Berg (“mountain”) + Werk (“works”).

verb:besudeln.tx: From Middle High German besudeln, besodeln, besodelen, equivalent to be- + Sudel (“puddle; muck”), from Middle Low German sudde (“swamp; marsh”). Akin to Middle High German sutte (“puddle; mudhole”), Old English ġesyd (“wallowing hole”).

noun:Blutvergießen.tx: Gerund of Blut vergießen (“to shed blood”). Equivalent to Blut + Vergießen.

verb:bewirten.tx: From Middle High German bewirten, equivalent to be- + Wirt + -en.

adj:bankrott.tx: From Italian banca rotta. More at bankrupt.

noun:Bankrott.tx: Around 1500. Borrowed from Italian banco rotto / Italian banca rotta. More at English bankrupt.

verb:brüllen.tx: From Middle High German brüelen, ultimately imitative. Compare Alemannic German brüele, Hunsrik brille, and Central Franconian brille.

noun:Baedeker.tx: Named after German publisher Karl Baedeker (1801–1859). The original spelling of the family name was Bädeker.

noun:Bagger.tx: From baggern through interpretation of the syllable -er- as the suffix -er.

noun:Bürokratie.tx: Borrowed from French bureaucratie. Equivalent to Büro + -kratie.

noun:Bewegung.tx: From Middle High German bewegunge, from Old High German biwegunga. Compare Dutch beweging and English beweighing. By surface analysis, bewegen + -ung.

intj:Bewegung.tx: From Middle High German bewegunge, from Old High German biwegunga. Compare Dutch beweging and English beweighing. By surface analysis, bewegen + -ung.

noun:Befund.tx: 17th c., deverbal from befinden. Also analysable as be- + Fund.

verb:berichten.tx: From Middle High German berihten (“to put in order; to instruct, to lecture”), from Old High German birihten (“to make correct”); equivalent to be- + richten.

noun:Bezirk.tx: From Middle High German bezirc, from be- + zirc, from Latin circus, itself from Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos, “circle, ring”).

verb:behüten.tx: From Middle High German behüeten, from Old High German bihuoten, from Proto-West Germanic *bihōdijan. Equivalent to be- + hüten.

noun:Bowle.tx: 18th century, from English bowl. Doublet of Bolle (“round object”).

verb:bügeln.tx: Back-formation from Bügeleisen (literally “iron with a bow, bail, handle”). By surface analysis, Bügel + -en.

pt: bent piece of metal; bow, bail, handle
noun:Bügeleisen.tx: From Bügel (“bent piece of metal; bow, bail, handle”) + Eisen (“iron”). Now commonly reanalyzed as bügeln (“to iron”) + Eisen, but the verb is in fact a backformation.

verb:begrüßen.tx: From Middle High German begrüeȥen, from Old High German bigruoȥen, bigruoȥȥen, from Proto-West Germanic *bigrōtijan; equivalent to be- + grüßen. Cognate with German Low German begröten, Dutch begroeten, West Frisian begroetsje, English begreet.

verb:beschneiden.tx: From Middle High German besnīden, from Old High German bisnīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *bisnīþan. Equivalent to be- + schneiden (“to cut”). Cognate with Dutch besnijden, Old English besnǣdan (“to cut, lop”). Compare also Old English besnyþian (“to deprive”).

verb:besetzen.tx: From Middle High German besetzen, from Old High German bisezzen, from Proto-West Germanic *bisattjan, from Proto-Germanic *bisatjaną (“to set near; set around”), equivalent to be- + setzen. Cognate with Saterland Frisian besätte, West Frisian besette, Dutch bezetten, English beset, German Low German besetten, Danish besætte, Swedish besätta.

noun:Bestie.tx: From Middle High German bestie, from Latin bēstia. Doublet of Biest n.

noun:Bergmann.tx: From Middle High German bercman, equivalent to Berg (“mountain”) + Mann (“man”).

noun:Beruf.tx: From Middle High German berufen. Deverbal from berufen (literally “calling”).

noun:Bestrafung.tx: From Middle High German bestrāfunge, equivalent to bestrafen + -ung.

noun:Balkon.tx: Borrowed from French balcon, from Italian balcone. Doublet of Balken.

noun:Basilikum.tx: From Late Latin basilicum, from Ancient Greek βᾰσῐλῐκός (băsĭlĭkós).

noun:Börse.tx: Borrowed from Dutch beurs, from Middle Dutch borse, from Old French borse (“purse”), from Late Latin bursa (“hide, purse”), from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa, “hide”).

adj:bescheiden.tx: From Middle High German bescheiden (“to assign; to inform”). By surface analysis, be- + scheiden. The adjective was originally the past participle.

verb:bescheiden.tx: From Middle High German bescheiden (“to assign; to inform”). By surface analysis, be- + scheiden. The adjective was originally the past participle.

noun:Beamter.tx: From Early New High German beampte (14th c.). Substantivization of beampt, haplologized participial adjective of beampten, which became beamten in New High German.

noun:Betrug.tx: From Middle High German betroc, from Old High German bitrog, from Proto-West Germanic *bidrog. The -u- is from German Trug, itself a back-formation from Middle High German trüge, from Old High German trugī, from the same Indo-European root.

verb:betrügen.tx: From Middle High German betriegen, from Old High German bitriogan, from Proto-West Germanic *bidreugan. Equivalent to be- + trügen. The modern -ü- in this verb chiefly follows the development in the rhyming word lügen (“to lie”). It was reinforced by the noun Betrug and by the 2nd and 3rd person-singular forms (as in lügen itself, which compare).

verb:befördern.tx: 16th century, from be- + fördern. Compare German Low German beföddern, befördern (from Middle Low German bevȫrderen), Dutch bevorderen. Compare also Middle High German gefordern, from Old High German gifordarōn.

verb:besitzen.tx: From Middle High German besitzen, from Old High German bisizzen, from Proto-West Germanic *bisittjan, from Proto-Germanic *bisitjaną, Equivalent to be- + sitzen. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål besitte, Danish besidde, Dutch bezitten, English besit, Swedish besitta, Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐍃𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (bisitan). (to own, to possess): Compare typologically Latin possideō (whence English possess), Macedonian поседува …

noun:Binsenweisheit.tx: From Binse (“rush”) + -n- + Weisheit (“wisdom”). Perhaps related to Latin nōdum in scirpō quaerere (literally “to look for a knot in the rushes”).

verb:benennen.tx: From Middle High German benennen, from Old High German *binemnen. Equivalent to be- + nennen. Cognate with Old Saxon binemnian, Old English benemnan. Compare English bename, Dutch benoemen, Swedish benämna.

noun:Bedingung.tx: From Middle High German bedingung, bedingunge. By surface analysis, bedingen + -ung.

adj:brenzlig.tx: From brenzeln (“to smell burnt”) + -ig, the former from brennen (“to burn”).

noun:Biest.tx: Via Middle Low German and/or West Central German from Middle Dutch beest, itself from Old French beste, from Latin bēstia. Doublet of Bestie.

verb:berechnen.tx: From Middle High German berëchenen, from Old High German birëhhanōn. Equivalent to be- + rechnen.

verb:bezahlen.tx: From Middle High German bezaln. By surface analysis, be- + zahlen. Compare Dutch betalen, Danish betale etc.

verb:bezichtigen.tx: Enhanced form of earlier bezichten (15th c.), denominal from now obsolete Bezicht (“accusation”), from Middle High German beziht, itself deverbal from Old High German bezīhan. Modern German bezeihen was gradually displaced, but is still attested until the early 20th century. The form with -ig- (16th c.) appears to be of northern origin; compare Middle Low German betichtigen (14th c.), Middle …

noun:Briefträger.tx: From Brief + tragen + -er resp. Brief + Träger.

adj:bizarr.tx: Late 17th century, from French bizarre, from Italian bizzarro. The chronology of earliest attestations suggests that it may have passed through Low German (mid-17th c.) and Dutch (early 17th c.), rather than being an immediate borrowing from French.

adj:bewusst.tx: Altered under the influence of gewusst from earlier bewist, from Middle High German bewissen (“to know all about, be conscious of, be aware of”), see wissen (“to know”).

noun:Biosphäre.tx: Coined by Austrian geologist Eduard Suess in 1875, from Ancient Greek βιος (bios) and σφαῖρα (sphaîra). By surface analysis, bio- + Sphäre.

noun:Basar.tx: Borrowed from French bazar, from Persian بازار (bâzâr) or a similar word in another Indo-Iranian language.

noun:Bildung.tx: From Middle High German bildunge, from Old High German bildunga. By surface analysis, bilden + -ung.

verb:begraben.tx: From Middle High German begraben, from Old High German bigraban, from Proto-Germanic *bigrabaną, equivalent to be- + graben.

verb:beschuldigen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German beschuldigen. Analyzable as be- + schuldig + -en

verb:besteuern.tx: From Middle High German bestiuren. By surface analysis, be- + Steuer + -n.

adj:begeistert.tx: From Geist (“ghost, spirit”). Cognate with Dutch begeesterd.

noun:Blamage.tx: From blamieren + -age, coined by German students from two French components.

adj:blamabel.tx: Mid 19th century, from French blâmable. By surface analysis, blamieren (“to embarrass; to disgrace oneself”) + -abel (“-able”).

noun:Badehose.tx: From baden (“to bath, swim”) + Hose (“trousers, shorts”).

verb:bedeuten.tx: From Middle High German bediuten, betiuten, from Old High German bidiuten. Equivalent to be- + deuten.

adj:blümerant.tx: 17th century, from French bleu mourant (“pale blue”, literally “dying blue, i.e. fading blue”). Altered under influence of German Blume (“flower”). The sense “unwell” from the change in complexion that may accompany such a state.

noun:Begierde.tx: From Middle High German begirde, from Old High German girida.

noun:Bürgersteig.tx: 19th century, from Bürger (“citizen”) + Steig (“footpath”). Introduced as a puristic alternative to then-predominant Trottoir (therefore unusual in Switzerland, like other purisms of that era).

adj:boshaft.tx: Ultimately from an umlaut-less byform of böse (compare also erbosen) + -haft, taking the place of earlier boshaftig.

verb:bezeichnen.tx: From Middle High German bezeichenen, from Old High German bizeihhanen, bizeihnen, from Proto-West Germanic *bitaiknijan. Equivalent to be- + zeichnen. Cognates include Dutch betekenen and English betoken.

verb:bemannen.tx: From Middle High German bemannen. Equivalent to be- + Mann + -en or be- + mannen.

verb:besuchen.tx: From Middle High German besuochen (“to seek, use, visit, investigate”), from Old High German bisuohhen (“to examine, check, try, inquire”), from Proto-West Germanic *bisōkijan. By surface analysis, be- + suchen. Cognate with Dutch bezoeken (“to visit, see”), Swedish besöka (“to visit, go to see”), English beseech (“to beg, enquire”).

verb:beäugen.tx: From Middle High German beougen, from Old High German biougen. Equivalent to be- + äugen.

verb:bohnern.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German bōnen, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to shine”). Cognate with Dutch boenen.

verb:befreien.tx: be- + frei (“free”) + -en. Compare with Swedish befria, English befree, Norwegian Bokmål befri, Dutch bevrijden.

adv:blanko.tx: From Italian bianco (“white, blank”), influenced by blank.

verb:blöken.tx: Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German bleken, ultimately imitative.

noun:Bernd.tx: Diminutive of Bernhard. The “anon” sense comes from the popular German imageboard Krautchan, where anonymous posters were known as Bernds.

noun:Barbarei.tx: Borrowed from Latin barbaria, equivalent to Barbar + -ei.

noun:Boje.tx: Via Middle Low German from early modern Dutch boye. Compare contemporary Dutch boei, English buoy.

noun:Bandit.tx: Borrowed from Italian bandito (“outlawed”), a derivative of Italian bandire (“to ban”).

noun:Broschüre.tx: In the 18th century, from French brochure.

verb:begehren.tx: From Middle High German begërn, prefixed form of earlier gërn, from Old High German gërōn. Related to gern (“willingly, gladly”). Cognate with Luxembourgish begieren. More at English yearn.

adj:blutig.tx: Blut (“blood”) + -ig (“-y”), or from Middle High German bluotec, bluotic.

noun:Begriff.tx: From Middle High German begrif (“region, area”). By surface analysis, deverbal from begreifen (“to understand, comprehend”). Cognate with Dutch begrip (“concept”) and Norwegian begrepet.

verb:ballen.tx: From Middle High German ballen, ultimately from the root of Ball. Probably cognate with English bale.

adj:blasiert.tx: With adaptation to a German past participle from French blasé, past participle of blaser, from Middle Dutch blâsen, from Proto-Germanic *blēsaną, whence German blasen. Compare semantically aufgeblasen, sich aufblähen.

noun:Behälter.tx: 15th c., behalten + -er. Compare earlier Middle High German behaltære and Old High German bihaltāri (“watcher, guardian, redeemer”) which yielded obsolete Behalter.

noun:Bodyguard.tx: Borrowed from English bodyguard, from body + guard.

noun:Blinddarm.tx: blind (“blind”) + Darm (“intestine”), a partial calque of Latin caecum (“blind (thing)”).

verb:beschließen.tx: From Middle High German beslieȥen, from Old High German bislioȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *bisleutan. Equivalent to be- + schließen. Cognate with Dutch besluiten and Luxembourgish beschléissen.

adj:bequem.tx: From Middle High German bequæme, bekōme (“suitable”), from Old High German biquāmi, derived from biqueman (whence German bekommen). The word seems originally to have been more common in Central and Low German; therefore possibly reinforced by cognate Middle Low German bequēme. The consonantism -qu-, which generally remained more stable in the north than it did in Upper German, may also point to …

verb:betteln.tx: From Middle High German betelen, from Old High German betalōn, from Proto-West Germanic *bedulōn. Despite superficial similarities in both word shape and meaning, not related to English peddle.

noun:Bettler.tx: From Middle High German betelære, from Old High German betalāri. See the verb betteln (“to beg”).

verb:blicken.tx: From Middle High German blicken, from Old High German blicchen, from Proto-West Germanic *blik, from Proto-Germanic *bliką (“look”).

noun:Blasebalg.tx: From blasen (“to blow”) + Balg (“animal hide; bellows”).

verb:brummen.tx: From Middle High German brummen, from Old High German *brummōn, from Proto-West Germanic *brummōn (“to drone, hum, growl”).

noun:Bö.tx: Borrowed from Dutch bui (which today usually refers to precipitation, not wind).

noun:Böller.tx: From Middle High German pöler or boler, originally referring to a mortar or catapult, from Middle High German boln (“to throw, to cast”), from Old High German bolôn (“to hurl”), related to bolla (“bud, bowl, bulbous thing”), from Proto-West Germanic *bollā, with the focus over time shifting towards the sound being made.

noun:Bankett.tx: Borrowed from Italian banchetto in the 15th century.

noun:Biwak.tx: Borrowed from French bivac, dated form of bivouac, from Alemannic German Biiwacht (“auxiliary watch or guard”). Doublet of dated German Beiwacht, Beiwache.

verb:biwakieren.tx: Borrowed from French bivouaquer. Analysable as Biwak + -ieren.

noun:Bombardement.tx: 18th century, from French bombardement. Equivalent to bombardieren + -ment.

noun:Bericht.tx: From Middle High German beriht, from Middle High German berihten, birihten, from Old High German birihten (“to straighten out, make tidy”), equivalent to be- + richten. Cognate with Middle Low German bericht (“report, doctrine, saying”), Dutch bericht.

noun:Bataillon.tx: Borrowed from French bataillon, from Italian battaglione.

noun:Ballen.tx: From Middle High German balle, from Old High German ballo, ultimately from the root of Ball. Cognate with Dutch baal, English bale, French balle.

verb:blitzen.tx: From earlier blickzen, from Middle High German bleczen, from Old High German blechazan, bleckezzen, blekkezzen, from Proto-West Germanic *blikkattjan (“to shine, glitter”).

noun:Bohrer.tx: From bohren (“to bore, drill”) + -er; compare Hunsrik Boher

noun:Brigade.tx: Borrowed from French brigade, from Italian brigata. Application to industrial work groups was influenced by Russian брига́да (brigáda) (itself a borrowing of this term).

pt: to stand, be on one's feet
verb:bestehen.tx: From Middle High German bestān, bestēn, from Old High German bistān, from Proto-Germanic *bistandaną, *bistāną. Equivalent to be- + stehen (“to stand, be on one's feet”).

noun:Buttersäure.tx: Calque of English butyric acid; Butter (“butter”) + Säure (“acid”).

noun:Bindewort.tx: From binden (“to bind, connect, tie”) + Wort (“word”),

noun:Bürde.tx: From a merger of Middle High German bürde and bürden, respectively from Old High German burdī and burdin, from Proto-West Germanic *burþī and *burþini, which last is also the source of English burden. The two forms were bound to merge because all Middle High German feminines in -en yield modern German -e (cf. Kette etc. and see Lüge for a similar merger).

noun:Besitz.tx: From Middle High German besitz (“seat, place”), from the verb besitzen (“to sit; to beseige”) (whence modern German besitzen (“to own, to possess”)).

conj:bevor.tx: From Middle High German bevor, bevorn, from Old High German bifora, biforan (“before”, adverb), from Proto-West Germanic *bifuranē. By surface analysis, be- + vor. Cognate with English before.

adv:bevor.tx: From Middle High German bevor, bevorn, from Old High German bifora, biforan (“before”, adverb), from Proto-West Germanic *bifuranē. By surface analysis, be- + vor. Cognate with English before.

verb:bedanken.tx: From be- + danken. Apparently not attested before Modern German (thus after 1400).

verb:boomen.tx: Borrowed from English boom. By surface analysis, Boom + -en.

verb:beeinträchtigen.tx: Not directly related to Eintracht (“concord, harmony”), but instead from another Eintracht, which was an East Central German variant of Eintrag (“impairment”). The earliest attestations of the verb are apparently from the 16th century. Regardless, both "Eintracht"s derive from the same root.

verb:bedauern.tx: From Middle High German betūren (also betiuren), a prefixation of tūren (“to consider grave”). Equivalent to modern be- + dauern (etymology 2), the simplex of which is now archaic. Pertaining to teuer (“dear, expensive”). The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German dūren).

verb:befehlen.tx: From Middle High German bevëlhen, from Old High German bifëlahan, bifëlhan, from Proto-West Germanic *bifelhan. Related to German empfehlen (“recommend, advocate”), but not German fehlen (“to be missing”).

noun:Blaupause.tx: From blau (“blue”) + Pause (“tracing”), a calque of English blueprint.

noun:Blutdruck.tx: From Blut (“blood”) + Druck (“pressure”). Compare Dutch bloeddruk, Swedish blodtryck, Danish blodtryk.

verb:beleuchten.tx: From Middle High German beliuhten, from Old High German biliuhten. Equivalent to be- + leuchten.

adj:blauäugig.tx: From blau + Auge + -ig. The metaphorical use (19th c.) is usually linked to the typically blue-eyed and fair-haired characters in naive, romanticist art. Compare blond (“stupid”). Perhaps the fact that newborns often have blue eyes may also be considered.

noun:Brise.tx: Via German Low German from French brise and/or English breeze. A Wanderwort of unknown origin.

noun:Bürgermeister.tx: From Middle High German burgermeister, bürgermeister, alongside the form burgemeister, bürgemeister. The former is equivalent to Bürger (“citizen”) + Meister (“master”), the latter to Burg (“city”) + Meister. It is uncertain which of the two forms is original. Compare Dutch burgemeester (Middle Dutch also with -er-). Compare also Burmeister.

adj:besessen.tx: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

noun:Backstein.tx: 17th century, from backen (“bake”) + Stein (“stone”), a calque of Middle Low German backstên.

noun:Bildhauer.tx: Bild + hauen + -er and Bild + Hauer. Note that the sense "to hew" is not the main meaning for the German word hauen.

verb:behindern.tx: From Middle High German behinderen, behindern. Equivalent to be- + hindern.

noun:Bunker.tx: Borrowed from English bunker (“large bin or container for storing coal; sand-pit hazard on a golf course”).
