adj:brachial.tx: Borrowed from Latin bracchialis, from bracchium (“arm”). The common sense from the use of the arms as a means of violence, as in a fist fight; probably reinforced by the phonetic similarity with brechen (“to break”, compare past tense brach).

noun:Beratung.tx: beraten + -ung. Cognate to archaic Dutch berading.

verb:beraten.tx: From Middle High German berāten, from Old High German birātan, from Proto-West Germanic *birādan. Equivalent to be- + raten. Cognate with obsolete English berede (“to advise”) and beread (“to inform, counsel, plan”) and Dutch beraden.

verb:behalten.tx: From Middle High German behalten, from Old High German bihaltan, from Proto-West Germanic *bihaldan. Equivalent to be- + halten. Cognates include Saterland Frisian behoolde (“to keep”), Dutch behouden (“to keep, restrain, preserve”), English behold, Danish and Norwegian beholde (“to keep”) and Swedish behålla (“to keep”).

noun:Bolle.tx: From Middle High German bolle, from Old High German bolla, from Proto-West Germanic *bollā, from Proto-Germanic *bullǭ.

verb:bereuen.tx: From Middle High German beriuwen, from Old High German biriuwēn, bihriuwēn. By surface analysis, be- + reuen.

adj:bravourös.tx: Borrowed from French bravoureux as Bravour + -ös.

noun:Ballon.tx: From French ballon, from Italian pallone (“balloon”, literally “large ball”), augmentative of palla (“ball”), which has the same Proto-Germanic root of Ball.

adj:bieder.tx: From Middle High German biderbe (also bederbe and shortened bider), from Old High German biderbi, piderpi, pidarpi, cognate with Bedarf. The derogatory sense arises in the 19th century. The compound Biedermann in origin means "brave, honest or capable man", but today has a meaning of "boring person, petty bourgeios".

noun:Bremer.tx: From Bremen + -er. The ending -en is sometimes lost before the suffix -er without there being a clear rule (compare -hausen, which makes -häuser or -hausener). The use for a sandwich is a pun on Hamburger.

adj:Bremer.tx: From Bremen + -er. The ending -en is sometimes lost before the suffix -er without there being a clear rule (compare -hausen, which makes -häuser or -hausener). The use for a sandwich is a pun on Hamburger.

noun:Bürzel.tx: From Early New High German bürtzel, pirtzel, a derivation of borzen, bürzen (“to protrude”). This may go back to Old High German bor (“summit, peak”), itself related to the verb bëran (“to bear”), as in the second element of empor (“upward”).

adj:berüchtigt.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German [Term?], related to rufen. See Gerücht for more.

verb:berufen.tx: From Middle High German berufen, berüefen, beruofen, from Old High German biruofōn, *biruofen, *biruofan, equivalent to be- + rufen. Cognate with German Low German beropen, Dutch beroepen, Saterland Frisian beroupe.

adv:bislang.tx: 16th century, originally in the longer form bissolang, a univerbation of bis (“until”) + so (“so”) + lang (“long”). The word was at first chiefly restricted to vernacular High German in northern Germany. It established itself more widely in the 19th century, but remains rare in Austria, Switzerland and South Tyrol.

noun:Beschwerde.tx: Inherited from Middle High German beswærde, from Old High German biswārida.

noun:Biskuit.tx: Borrowed from French biscuit. Doublet of Biskotte.

noun:Bildungsroman.tx: From Bildung (“formation”) + -s- + Roman (“novel”), literally “novel of education”; coined by Johann Karl Simon Morgenstern c. 1820, writing Über das Wesen des Bildungsromans (“On the Nature of the Bildungsroman”).

noun:Buchweizen.tx: Buche + Weizen. A calque of Middle Low German bōkwete.

verb:bereiten.tx: From Middle High German bereiten, from Old High German bireiten. By surface analysis, bereit + -en.

verb:begehen.tx: From Middle High German begēn, begān, from Old High German bigēn, bigān, from Proto-West Germanic *bigān. Equivalent to be- + gehen. Cognates include Dutch begaan and English bego.

noun:Besonderheit.tx: By surface analysis, besonders + -heit. Compare Swedish besynnerlighet.

verb:beschatten.tx: From Middle High German beschatewen, beschetwen, from Old High German biskatawen, from Proto-West Germanic *biskadwijan. Equivalent to be- + schatten. Cognates include Dutch beschaduwen and English beshadow.

noun:Bewusstsein.tx: bewusst (“aware, conscious”) + sein (“to be”). The word became common in speech through the influence of Martin Luther, who used it frequently.

verb:behagen.tx: From Middle High German behagen, related to Old High German gihagin (“cherished”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bihagōną, from *hagō-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱak- (“to be able”), see also Avestan 𐬯𐬀𐬐- (sak-, “to agree”). Cognates include Dutch behagen, Old Saxon bihagon and Old English gehagian.

verb:beseitigen.tx: From now obsolete beseit (“aside”) (compare modern beiseite) + -igen.

noun:Beifuß.tx: From Middle High German bīvuoz, bībōz, from Old High German pīpōz, bībōz, bīvōz, bīvūz, probably from bī- + bōzan (“to push, to strike”), from Proto-West Germanic *bautan, from Proto-Germanic *bautaną. The semantic development remains unclear. The v-form with folk-etymological adaptation to vuoz (“foot”) is attested since the 10th century, apparently at first in West Central German, where the …

verb:bemerken.tx: From Middle High German bemerken, from Old High German bimerken, from Proto-West Germanic *bimarkijan. Equivalent to be- + merken. Cognate with Dutch bemerken, also related to Middle Dutch and Middle High German bemarken, and English bemark.

adj:brandneu.tx: Ca. 1930, from Brand (“fire, burning”) + neu (“neu”), after English brand new (originally “fresh from the fire”, as of a piece of metal). It is possible that German Brand goes back to phono-semantic matching of English brand rather than true loan translation, seeing that the archaic sense “fire” is not widely known among German learners of English. This would mean that the original sense of the …

noun:Beichtvater.tx: From Middle High German bīhtvater. Analysable as Beichte (“confession”) + Vater (“father”).

verb:bestreiten.tx: From Middle High German bestrīten (“to fight against”), equivalent to be- + streiten. Compare English bestride. The sense “to pay” comes from the notion of “be able to cope with”.

noun:Beige.tx: From late Middle High German bīge, from Old High German bīga, pīga, further origin uncertain. Cognate with Alemannic German Biigi.

noun:Bronze.tx: 16th century as Bronzo, Brunzo, directly from Italian bronzo. Since the 18th century adapted to French bronze, itself from the Italian. Further origin uncertain; see the Italian lemma for more. The unusual pronunciation /s/ for ‹z› perhaps developed as a compromise between French /z/ and German /ts/.

verb:bleichen.tx: From a merger of Middle High German bleichen, from Old High German bleihhen, from Proto-West Germanic *blaikijan, from Proto-Germanic *blaikijaną, and Middle High German blīchen, from Old High German blīhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *blīkan, from Proto-Germanic *blīkaną. Related to bleich. Cognate with Dutch bleken and blijken, English bleach and blike, Danish blege.

noun:Bereitschaft.tx: From Middle High German bereitschaft. Equivalent to bereit + -schaft.

noun:Bekenntnis.tx: From Middle High German bekentnisse, bekantnisse f, from Old High German bikantnussi n. By surface analysis, bekennen + -nis. Compare Dutch bekentenis.

verb:bekennen.tx: From Middle High German bekennen, from Old High German bikennen, from Proto-West Germanic *bikannijan. Equivalent to be- + kennen. Cognates include Dutch bekennen, and English and Scots beken.

noun:Betrieb.tx: A calque of Middle Low German bedrîf, like the underlying verb betreiben (from bedrîven). The noun is closer to the Low German form because of the preserved monophthong (instead of *Betreib). See the regular development in cognate Dutch bedrijf.

adj:blutrünstig.tx: From Middle High German bluotrünstec, bluotrunsec (“strongly bleeding”), derived from bluotruns (“strongly bleeding wound”) (modern German Blutrunst), from bluot (“blood”) + runs (“flow of water”), the latter being related with German rinnen (“to run”, of a fluid). Analysable in modern German as Blut (“blood”) + Runse (“bed of a mountain stream”) + -ig. The word Runse is restricted to Alpine …

noun:Beryll.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin bēryllus. Doublet of Brille, a borrowing from Old French.

verb:begreifen.tx: From Middle High German begrīfen, from Old High German bigrīfan, from Proto-West Germanic *bigrīpan. Equivalent to be- + greifen. Compare English begripe, begrip, Low German begriepen and Dutch begrijpen.

verb:beheben.tx: From Middle High German beheben (“to take away”), equivalent to be- + heben.

noun:Baumwolle.tx: From Middle High German boumwolle, from Late Old High German boumwolla. By surface analysis, Baum (“tree”) + Wolle (“wool”). Perhaps based on Herodotus’ description of wool-bearing trees in India; compare Ancient Greek ἐριόξυλον (erióxulon, “cotton”, literally “wood/tree-wool”) and Latin linum xylinum (“cotton”, literally “wood/tree-flax”).

noun:Buchs.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German buhs, from Proto-West Germanic *buhs, from Latin buxus. Cognate with Middle Dutch bos, English box.

verb:beschweren.tx: From Middle High German beswæren (“to afflict, to depress, to annoy”), a merger from Old High German biswāren (“to depress, to burden”) (10th c.), from Proto-West Germanic *biswârijan; and Old High German biswārōn (“to burden”) (10th c.), from Proto-West Germanic *biswārōn. Related to swāren (“heavy”) (8th c.) whence schwer. The reflexive sense developed later in the 14th century from "to burden …

noun:Bresche.tx: Borrowed from French brèche. Doublet of Brekzie.

noun:Bitumen.tx: From Latin bitūmen. Doublet of Beton.

verb:beamen.tx: Borrowed from English beam in the science fiction sense, popularised by the series Star Trek (first broadcast in Germany in 1972). The sense “to project” is a figurative use, apparently since the 1990s. Doublet of Baum.

noun:Büste.tx: * The word was borrowed from Italian busto and French buste in the 18th century: More precisely, at the beginning of the 18th century the Busto and Buste were borrowed from Italian busto, and since the 2nd half of the 18th century, under influence of French buste which was also borrowed from Italian, the German word Büste was applied in general use. Further details about the origin are not …

verb:bewirken.tx: From Middle High German bewirken, bewürken, from Old High German biwurken. Equivalent to be- + wirken.

noun:Beiwort.tx: From bei (“by, at”) + Wort (“word”). * For the sense adjective cf. Beinennwort and beiständiges Nennwort. * For the sense adverb cf. Dutch bijwoord.

adj:bemitleidenswert.tx: bemitleiden (“to feel compassion”) + -wert (“-worthy”), ultimately derived from Mitleid (“compassion”).

verb:büffeln.tx: According to Kluge, from Büffel (“buffalo”), from its use as a working animal. Pfeifer considers it to have originally been an intensive form of büffen (“to puff, to push”), obsolete alternative form of puffen, with the meaning gained by folk-etymological association with Büffel.

noun:Baldrian.tx: From Middle High German baldriān (also: waldriān), from Old High German baldriān. Compare Middle Low German boldriān. Seemingly together with Hungarian bojtorján (“burdock”) (√ *boltorján) loaned in the Dark Age period from the late 6ᵗʰ to early 8ᵗʰ century from Turkic or Proto-Mongolic, the Pannonian Avars being direct neighbours to the Germans, cognate to Turkish بالدران / baldıran (“hemlock”) …

verb:begegnen.tx: From Middle High German begegenen, begagenen, from Old High German bigaganen, with prefix from Proto-West Germanic *gaginijan, from Proto-Germanic *gaginjaną; equivalent to be- + gegnen (“encounter”) + -en. Cognate with Dutch bejegenen.

noun:Blutgruppe.tx: From Blut (“blood”) + Gruppe (“group, category”); perfectly analogous to cognate Dutch bloedgroep, Swedish blodgrupp.

adj:blutrot.tx: From Middle High German bluotrōt, from Old High German, from Proto-Germanic *blōþaraudaz (whence also English bloodred). Analysable as Blut (“blood”) + rot (“red”).

noun:Bienenkorb.tx: Biene (“bee”) + -n- + Korb (“basket”) (from Latin corbis of unclear, perhaps Germanic origin); perfectly parallel to Dutch equivalent bijenkorf

noun:Bückling.tx: From Middle High German bückinc, borrowed from Middle Low German bückink. Pertaining to Bock (“buck”), seemingly because of the pungent smell.

verb:besprechen.tx: From Middle High German besprechen, from Old High German besprechan, besprehhan (also bisprechōn, bisprehhōn), from Proto-Germanic *bisprekaną (“to speak about, discuss, blame”), equivalent to be- + sprechen. Cognate with English bespeak, Dutch bespreken, West Frisian besprekke.

noun:Balsam.tx: From Middle High German balsam, balsame, from Old High German balsamo, from Proto-West Germanic *balsamō. Doublet of Bisam and Desman.

verb:belagern.tx: From be- + Lager + -en. Compare English beleaguer, Dutch belegeren, Luxembourgish belageren.

noun:Bachen.tx: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

noun:Baracke.tx: Borrowed from French baraque, from Catalan barraca.

verb:beschämen.tx: From Middle High German beschemen. Equivalent to be- + schämen.

verb:belegen.tx: From Middle High German belegen, from Old High German bileggen. By surface analysis, be- + legen. Cognate with English belay.

verb:beziehen.tx: From Middle High German beziehen, from Old High German biziohan, from Proto-West Germanic *biteuhan. Equivalent to be- + ziehen. The sense “to refer” is probably influenced by Latin referre. Compare Dutch betrekken.

adv:blindlings.tx: Equivalent to blind + -lings. The formation is old; compare Old High German blintilingon.

verb:betrachten.tx: From Middle High German betrahten, from Old High German bitrahtōn, bitrahten. Equivalent to be- + trachten. Cognate with Dutch betrachten.

noun:Bananenrepublik.tx: From Banane (“banana”) + -n- + Republik (“republic”), calque of English banana republic.

noun:Bratze.tx: Borrowed from Italian braccio (“arm”), from Latin brachium, bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn). Doublet of Bratsche.

verb:besorgen.tx: From Middle High German besorgen, from Old High German bisorgēn. By surface analysis, be- + sorgen. Compare Dutch bezorgen, English besorrow.

noun:Bestattung.tx: From Middle High German bestatunge. By surface analysis, bestatten + -ung.

noun:Beschluss.tx: Nominal formation related to beschließen (“to decide”).

noun:Bogenschießen.tx: From Bogen (“arc, arch, bow”) + schießen (“to shoot”). Compare Dutch boogschieten.

noun:Bratsche.tx: From Bratschgeige, from Italian viola da braccio, from viola and braccio (“arm”), from Latin bracchium. Doublet of Bratze.

noun:Brandung.tx: Borrowed from Dutch branding (also attested as Branding in German).

adv:beinahe.tx: From Middle High German bīnāhe, bīnāch. Analysable as bei (“by, near”) + nah (“near, close”). Compare Dutch bijna.

verb:blinzeln.tx: From Middle High German blinzeln. Related to blinken (“to gleam, to twinkle”). Cognate with Luxembourgish blënzelen.

noun:Brühwürfel.tx: From brühen (“to blanch; to brew”) + Würfel (“cube”).

adv:baldmöglichst.tx: From bald (“soon”) + möglich (“possible”) + -st (superlative ending). Constructs of this kind usually take the superlative ending on the first component. Compare the related terms below, for which the variants frühmöglichst, schnellmöglichst are attested, but uncommon. The reverse tendency in the case of baldmöglichst probably has to do with the fact that a superlative am *baldesten does not exist.

noun:Brieftaube.tx: From Brief (“letter (writing)”) + Taube (“dove [cognate], pigeon”); compare Dutch postduif.

noun:Balustrade.tx: Borrowed from French balustrade, from Italian.

adv:bisschen.tx: Adverbialized noun Bisschen, from Bissen (“a bit, bite”) + -chen (diminutive suffix)

noun:Bader.tx: From Middle High German badære, from Old High German batheri. Originally, the Bader was the owner of the bath house. Later the meaning of the word was extended to other professions. Doublet of Bad.

adj:besoffen.tx: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form. Compare also Dutch bezopen.

noun:Bims.tx: From Middle High German pümeze, bümez, bimz, from Old High German pumiz, from Proto-West Germanic *pumic (“pumice stone”).

verb:bewahren.tx: Inherited from Middle High German bewarn, from Old High German biwarōn, from Proto-Germanic *biwarōną. By surface analysis, be- + wahren, see the latter for more. Cognate with English beware.

noun:Butterfass.tx: From Middle High German *butervaz (attested 15th c. as bottervais, putterfas). By surface analysis, Butter (“butter”) + Fass (“vat, barrel”).

noun:Biotop.tx: From bio- + -top, from Ancient Greek τόπος (tópos, “area; place”).

verb:begründen.tx: From Middle High German begründen (“to found, solidify”). Equivalent to be- + gründen (“to establish, build”). The figurative meaning of reason comes from Grund.

verb:bangen.tx: From Middle High German bangen, pangen, from Middle High German bange (“fear”). Compare Middle High German angen (“to fear”). More at bang.

verb:befinden.tx: From Middle High German bevinden, from Old High German bifindan, from Proto-West Germanic *bifinþan. Equivalent to be- + finden.

verb:blubbern.tx: Of onomatopoeic origin. Compare the associated interjection blubb, and glucken, gluckern representing similar sounds.

adj:bleich.tx: From Middle High German bleich, from Old High German bleih, from Proto-West Germanic *blaik.

verb:benehmen.tx: From Middle High German benëmen, from Old High German binëman, from Proto-West Germanic *bineman, from Proto-Germanic *binemaną. Equivalent to be- + nehmen. Compare English benim.

verb:bannen.tx: From Middle High German bannen, from Old High German bannan, from Proto-West Germanic *bannan, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną.

noun:Baumgarten.tx: Baum + Garten, literally “tree garden”. Doublet of Bungert.

pt: to roast, to bake, to fry
noun:Bratkartoffeln.tx: braten (“to roast, to bake, to fry”) + Kartoffeln (“potatoes”)

verb:bedingen.tx: From Middle High German bedingen (“to hire (especially for a crime)”), synchronically be- + dingen. The modern senses are influenced by and almost a back-formation from Bedingung (“condition”).

adj:bescheuert.tx: From scheuern as in jemandem eine scheuern (“to slap/smack someone”), therefore originally “(having been) slapped” or “smacked”.

verb:bummeln.tx: 17th century, for “to swing, waver” (of the clapper of a bell), iterative formation from onomatopoeic bim-bam-bum for the sound of a bell; compare bimmeln (“to ring”). From this Low German bummeln (18th c.) in the contemporary sense. Related with baumeln (likely an alteration after Baum) and Bommel (“bobble”).

noun:Bakschisch.tx: Via English baksheesh or French bakchich.

noun:Bohnenkraut.tx: From Bohne (“bean”) + Kraut (“herb”). So named because savory in German cuisine is used especially with beans (green beans as well as broad beans). Compare Dutch bonenkruid.

verb:bemühen.tx: From be- + Mühe + -en. Compare Dutch bemoeien.

verb:blättern.tx: From Middle High German bleteren, synchronically analyzed as Blatt + -ern.

verb:bewerben.tx: From Middle High German bewërben, from Old High German biwërban, from Proto-West Germanic *bihwerban. Equivalent to be- + werben.

noun:Büttel.tx: From Middle High German bütel, butel, from Old High German butil (“court official, messenger”), from Proto-West Germanic *budil, from Proto-Germanic *budilaz (“herald, messenger”), from Proto-Germanic *beudaną (“to announce, present, offer”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“to make aware”). Akin to Swedish bödel and Old English bydel (“beadle”). More at beadle.

noun:Brailleschrift.tx: From Braille + Schrift (“alphabet”), named after Louis Braille.

noun:Balg.tx: From Middle High German balc, from Old High German balg, from Proto-West Germanic *balgi. Words for inflated objects are often used to refer to children; compare western German Panz (“child”), which is related with Pansen (“rumen”). Cognates Cognate with Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐌻𐌲𐍃 (balgs, “wineskin”), Dutch balg, English belly, bellows. Compare also Russian балка (balka, “thick plank”), Slovene blazina …

noun:Backfisch.tx: From backen (“to bake”) + Fisch (“fish”). Figurative sense probably from the use of younger, smaller fish for baking, although many different theories exist.

verb:brühen.tx: From Middle High German brüen, brüejen (“to brew, singe, burn”), from Old High German *bruojan (“to scald, burn”), from Proto-Germanic *brōaną (“to brew”) and related *brewwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerw-, *bʰrew- (“to boil, seethe”). Cognates Cognate with Middle Dutch broeyen (“to heat”), Old French bruir (“to burn”), Old High German briuwan (“to brew”). More at brew.

noun:Buchhalter.tx: From Buch halten (“to keep the books”) + -er. This verbal phrase is now rare. For some reason one usually says Buchhalter, but Buch führen. For the action noun both Buchhaltung and Buchführung are common. Further analysable as Buch (“book”) + halten (“to hold”) + -er (agent suffix).

noun:Boss.tx: In the contemporary form (19th c.) chiefly from English boss, partly also from older northern German Baas (17th c.), both eventually from Dutch baas.

noun:Bistum.tx: From Middle High German bistuom, a contraction of bischoptuom, from Old High German biscoptuom, from biscop (“bishop”) + -tuom; equivalent to Bischof + -tum. Cognate with Dutch bisdom, German Low German Bischopdom, English bishopdom.

noun:Bissen.tx: From Middle High German bizze, from Old High German bizzo, from Proto-Germanic *bitô. See the verb *bītaną (“to bite”). Cognate with Old English bita. In Dutch beet, English bit, this word has been merged with Proto-Germanic *bitiz, whence German Biss. (English bite is a new derivation from the verb.)

noun:Bigamie.tx: From Latin bi- + Ancient Greek γάμος (gámos, “marriage”), equivalent to bi- + -gamie.

adj:buchbar.tx: Derived from the verb buchen: buch- (“book”) + -bar (“-able”).

noun:Brodem.tx: With widespread dialectal -ā- → -ō- from Middle High German brādem, from Old High German brādam, from Proto-West Germanic *brāþm, probably a secondary alteration of *brāþi by conflation with *āþm, whence German Atem, Odem. Cognate with English breath.

verb:begeben.tx: be- + geben. Cognate with English begive.

noun:Barmann.tx: From Bar (“bar”) + Mann (“man”), a partial calque of English barman.

noun:Banshee.tx: Borrowed from English banshee, from Irish bean sí, from Old Irish ben síde (literally “woman of the fairy mound”).

noun:Bittersüß.tx: bitter + süß. Compare Dutch bitterzoet, English bittersweet.

noun:Brikett.tx: Borrowed from French briquette. Doublet of brechen.

verb:bocken.tx: From Middle High German bocken, equivalent to Bock + -en.

verb:betragen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German betragen and independent formations from be- + tragen

adv:bergauf.tx: From Berg + auf. Compare Luxembourgish biergop.

adv:bergab.tx: From Berg + ab. Compare Luxembourgish biergof.

noun:Barte.tx: Pertaining to Bart (“beard”). The form is most probably from the Dutch plural baarden, although contemporary Dutch uses balein.

verb:bewältigen.tx: From be- + waltig + -en, in which waltig is an obsolete variant of gewaltig.

verb:beschwören.tx: From Middle High German beswern, from Old High German biswerian (“to beg solemnly, ceremoniously, urgently or emphaticly”). Equivalent to be- + schwören. Cognate with Dutch bezweren and Middle Low German besweren (whence Swedish besvärja, Danish besværge and Norwegian Bokmål besverge).

adj:benommen.tx: From etymology 1 specifically in the now archaic sense of "to take away", probably from the idea of being "bereft of one's senses". The past participle being applied to the person and not to what was taken is unusual, but historically there was also a usage of the verb with the person as the accusative object and that which was taken as a genitive object, as in (and perhaps influenced by) berauben.

noun:Bluff.tx: Borrowed from French bluff, from English bluff. Compare German verblüffen.

verb:bluffen.tx: Borrowed from English bluff. See the noun Bluff for more.

noun:Beschützer.tx: From beschützen + -er, from: be- (“forming verbs with the sense of working towards something”) + schützen (“shut away: guard, protect”), and from -er (“-er: forming agent nouns”).

verb:blecken.tx: From Middle High German blecken, from Old High German blecchen, ultimately related to a factitive Proto-West Germanic *blīkan (“to shine”).

noun:Baba.tx: From a Slavic language. Compare Polish baba (“grandmother”), Russian баба (baba, “grandma”).

adj:besondere.tx: From (late) Middle High German besunder, from bi + sunder. See also sonder.

verb:betreten.tx: From Middle High German betrëten, from Old High German bitrëtan, from Proto-West Germanic *bitredan. Equivalent to be- + treten.

adj:bekloppt.tx: Past participle of the rarer verb bekloppen (“to hit on", "to percuss”), thus “insane as if beaten in the head”. Related to kloppen (“to hit”), the Central and German Low German form of klopfen (“to knock”).

noun:Bai.tx: Borrowed from Dutch baai, which probably from French baie. Further origin uncertain.

noun:Bommel.tx: Initially North and West German variation of Bummel, from bummeln in the original sense of "to dangle". The permeation of the alternative vocalism across most of the language area was perhaps motivated by distinction from the re-derivation of Bummel (“(lazy) stroll”) from the modern sense of the verb, forming a doublet.

noun:Bijou.tx: Borrowed from French bijou, itself borrowed from Breton bizou (“ring”).

noun:Bakteriologie.tx: From bakterio- + -logie, ultimately from Ancient Greek βακτήριον (baktḗrion, “little rod”), from βάκτρον (báktron, “rod, staff, stick”) + λόγος (lógos, “word, reason”).

adj:bairisch.tx: Spelling variant of bayrisch, later functionalized in linguistic terminology.

verb:bekehren.tx: From Middle High German bekēren, from Old High German bikēren, from Proto-West Germanic *bikaizjan.

verb:beunruhigen.tx: From be- + unruhig + -en. Compare Luxembourgish beonrouegen.

verb:bescheinigen.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German beschênigen (14th c.), extended form of beschênen, from be- + Proto-West Germanic *skainijan (“to make appear”). This latter verb is a causative of *skīnan, whence German scheinen (“to shine, appear”). It was borrowed along the Lower Rhine in the 15th century and fully established itself in High German during the 16th. Due to the merger of West Germanic ai and ī, …

verb:beschlagnahmen.tx: End of 19th century, from Beschlagnahme, verbal noun of in Beschlag nehmen.

noun:Bummel.tx: Back-formation from bummeln. Doublet of Bommel.

verb:bumsen.tx: From the onomatopoeic interjection bums, bum + -sen (iterative suffix). The sexual sense rose to prominence in the mid of the twentieth century, when before rumsen was used the same way, now not known any more.

noun:Busserl.tx: From Buss (“kiss”) + -erl (“-ie”). The first element is of onomatopoeic origin; compare Central Franconian Butz (“kiss”) and similar forms in many languages. See Czech pusa, Serbo-Croatian pusa, maybe related to Proto-Indo-European *bus- (“to kiss”).

noun:Brandschatzung.tx: Brandschatz + -ung. 16th-century recharacterization of the earlier (Middle High German) synonym Brandschatz. The original meaning of the term is "exaction of tribute under the threat of pillaging". The shift to the now-prevalent meaning of "looting, pillaging" takes place in the 20th century, apparently by misunderstanding, but this usage is now sanctioned by the Duden, which glosses the term as …

noun:Bestand.tx: From Middle High German bestant, equivalent to be- + Stand. Cognate with Dutch bestand, German Low German Bestahn, Bestand, West Frisian bestân.

noun:Bong.tx: From English bong, from Thai บ้อง (bɔ̂ng). Feminine gender after Pfeife (“pipe”).

noun:Bulli.tx: Blend of Bus + Lieferwagen, or from bullig.

noun:Broiler.tx: Borrowed from English broiler around 1960. The exact way this term found its way into East German terminology is uncertain and subject to debate. Due to general economic problems, East Germany was dependent on foodstuff imports throughout its history; one possibility therefore is that chickens were at one point imported from Anglophone countries, e.g. the USA. Another theory instead suggests that …

noun:Bakterie.tx: From New Latin bacteria, plural of bacterium reinterpreted as feminine singular. See also Bakterium.

noun:Bürgerschaft.tx: From Middle High German bürgerschaft, equivalent to Bürger (“citizen”) + -schaft (“-ship, -ry”). The sense “municipal parliament” after Middle Low German börgerschop (“municipal council”). Compare also Dutch burgerschap.

noun:Bundesliga.tx: From Bund (“federation”) + -es- + Liga (“league”), thus “federal league”, in the sense of “nationwide league”.

verb:beschäftigen.tx: From Middle High German scheftec (“active”), possibly under the influence of Low German bescheftich (“bustling, industrious”); see the related schaffen for more.

verb:beeindrucken.tx: From the compounding of the inseparable Old High German be- + eindrucchane (today eindrücken), from the compounding of the Old High German prefix ein- + drucchen.

verb:beherrschen.tx: From be- + herrschen. Compare Dutch beheersen and Yiddish באַהערשן (bahershn).

noun:Belt.tx: From Danish bælt, from Latin Baltia, a mythological island described by Pliny the Elder in his Natural History, of unclear origin. It bears no relation to Danish bælte (“belt”), which is derived from Latin balteus (“belt, girdle”) and for which the German word is Gürtel. Possibly instead related to Lithuanian baltas (“white”).

verb:bejahen.tx: 16th century, equivalent to be- + ja (“yes”) + -en (with -h- as orthographic hiatus breaker). While the verb may have been derived directly from the interjection ja, an alternative possibility is that it is a reinterpretation of Middle High German bejëhen (“to acknowledge, admit”), from jëhen (“to say”). The according spelling bejähen is indeed attested in the 17th century.

noun:Bärlauch.tx: From Bär (“bear”) + Lauch (“leek”). Calque of Latin Allium ursīnum (literally “bear garlic”).

noun:Beamtin.tx: Irregular formation from beamt (“holding an office”) + -in (“suffix for female nouns”). The regular female nominalisation of beamt is Beamte, the suffix -in is not normally attached to nominalisations from adjectives.

adj:burschikos.tx: Jocular compound of German Bursche and Ancient Greek -ικός (-ikós).

verb:beachten.tx: From Middle High German beahten, from Old High German biahtōn (“to account for, to classify as, to bethink”). Equivalent to be- + achten.

verb:belaufen.tx: From Middle High German beloufen. Equivalent to be- + laufen. Cognate with Dutch belopen.

adj:belaufen.tx: From Middle High German beloufen. Equivalent to be- + laufen. Cognate with Dutch belopen.

noun:Baumkuchen.tx: From Baum (“tree”) + Kuchen (“cake”), because the concentric-ring layers resemble tree rings.

noun:Beisein.tx: Deverbal from beisein, from Middle High German bīsīn, from Old High German bīsīn.

noun:Behältnis.tx: From Middle High German beheltnisse, behaltnisse f, from Old High German bihaltnessi n. By surface analysis, behalten + -nis.

verb:benetzen.tx: From Middle High German benetzen, from Old High German binezzen, derived from nezzen, from Proto-West Germanic *nattjan, from Proto-Germanic *natjaną, from *nataz (“wet”), whence German nass. Equivalent to be- + netzen, which simplex is highly archaic. The relation with nass is typically not recognised by contemporary speakers, who may in fact associate it with Netz (“net”), as if meaning “to …

verb:beschaffen.tx: 15th century, from be- + schaffen. Formally from Old High German biskaffōn (“to create, form”) since it also had a weak declension. Middle High German beschaffen is formally related, but had a strong declension. The base lemma schaffen had both a strong and a weak paradigm (which are both continued in modern schaffen).

adj:beschaffen.tx: From Middle High German beschaffen. Possibly a continuation of an unattested Old High German *biskaffan. Obsolete since Early New High German, but the past participle is continued as adjective.

verb:bedürfen.tx: From Middle High German bedürfen, bedurfen, from Old High German bidurfan (“need, require”). By surface analysis, be- + dürfen.

verb:bestücken.tx: From be- + Stück + -en; first attested in the 18th century.

verb:beschlafen.tx: From Middle High German beslāfen, equivalent to be- + schlafen.

noun:Body.tx: Borrowed from French body, and this a pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of English bodysuit.

noun:Blauer.tx: Substantivisation of the adjective blau. "Policeman" sense from the blue uniforms; currency senses from the color of the bills.

adj:befindlich.tx: From Middle High German bevindelich. Equivalent to befinden + -lich.

noun:Binder.tx: From binden (“to bind, to fasten”) + -er (“-er: forming agent nouns”)

noun:Bleiche.tx: From Middle High German bleiche, from Old High German bleih, from Proto-West Germanic *blaik.

noun:Brokkoli.tx: 18th century, from Italian broccoli, which see. The usual pronunciation with a long /oː/ is perhaps influenced by the French spelling brocoli, formerly also found in German texts. The sense of "marijuana" originated from a widely mocked quote said by the former German federal drug commissioner Daniela Ludwig at a press conferrence in 2020. : "Nur weil Alkohol gefährlich ist, unbestritten, ist …

noun:Beauftragter.tx: Substantivization of beauftragt, past participle of beauftragen.

noun:Bekanntmachung.tx: bekannt + Machung, or substantivisation of bekanntmachen (“make public”).

noun:Bollwerk.tx: From Middle Low German and Middle Dutch bolwerk.

verb:betreuen.tx: From Middle High German betriuwen. By surface analysis, be- + treu + -en.

noun:Beschäftigter.tx: From beschäftigt (“busy; employed”) + -er; a substantivization of beschäftigt, past participle of beschäftigen.

verb:büßen.tx: From Middle High German büeȥen, from Old High German buoȥen, buoȥȥen, from Proto-West Germanic *bōtijan.

verb:bezaubern.tx: From Middle High German bezoubern, from Old High German bizoubarōn, from Proto-West Germanic *bitaubrōn. Equivalent to be- + zaubern. Cognate with Dutch betoveren.

noun:Blag.tx: From German Low Franconian and western dialects of German Low German. Akin to Dutch blaag (“kid”). Ultimately of unknown origin.

verb:befürchten.tx: From Middle High German befürhten, bevürhten, from Old High German biforhten, bifurihtōn, biforhtōn, biforahtōn, from Proto-West Germanic *bifurhtijan, *bifurhtōn, equivalent to be- + fürchten. Cognate with Middle Low German bevrüchten, English befright.

noun:Beize.tx: From Middle High German beize, from Old High German beiza, from Proto-Germanic *baitō. The word originally had a fricative (Beiße, Old High German beiʒa); the form with an affricate under influence of the verb beizen.

verb:bedrucken.tx: From Middle High German bedrücken, from Old High German bidrukken, from Proto-West Germanic *biþrukkijan. Doublet of bedrücken. The usage of the umlaut-less Upper German variant as technical term for (im)printing established in the 17th century. Equivalent to be- + drucken.

pt: burgher, member of the middle class
noun:Bürgerhaus.tx: Bürger (“burgher, member of the middle class”) + Haus (“house”)

verb:begnügen.tx: be- + genügen with syncope of the second e.

verb:bescheren.tx: From Middle High German beschern (“to preordain, destine, allot, distribute”), from Old High German biskerren, biskerien, from a prefixed formation related to Proto-West Germanic *skeran (“to shear”), with sense development "divide, cut" > "allocate" > "give (Christmas gifts)". Compare Yiddish באַשערט (bashert, “predestined”).

noun:Belang.tx: From Middle High German belanc, itself a deverbal back-formation from belangen.

noun:Besteck.tx: From bestecken (“to provide a thing by inserting it into another thing”), from be- + stecken. Originally referred to a case into which a set of tools was put, later shifting to refer to the tools themselves.

noun:Bot.tx: Clipping of Roboter, influenced by English bot.

verb:besinnen.tx: From Middle High German besinnen; equivalent to be- + sinnen.

noun:Barke.tx: From Middle High German barke, borrowed via Middle Dutch barke from Middle French barque, from Old French barque, from Late Latin barca.

verb:bekunden.tx: Borrowed from German Low German, from be- + kunden, Central German form of künden (“to announce, tell”).

verb:belangen.tx: From Middle High German belangen, blangen, from Old High German belangēn, from Proto-West Germanic *bilangōn. By surface analysis, be- + langen.

noun:Blähung.tx: From Middle High German blæjunge. By surface analysis, blähen + -ung.

noun:Beiz.tx: Rotwelsch, from Yiddish בית (beys, “house”), itself from Hebrew בַּיִת (báyit). Compare Alemannic German Beiz.

noun:Buhle.tx: From Middle High German buole, puole, from *buolo, *puolo, from Proto-Germanic *bō- (“male relative, kinsman”). Cognate with Middle Low German bōle, Dutch boel. More at bully.

adj:blödsinnig.tx: blöd + -sinnig, formed in the 17th century with the meaning “mentally impaired”, which is no longer valid.

prep:betreffs.tx: From genitive singular of Betreff (“subject”). Compare mangels (“for lack of”), from genitive singular of Mangel (“lack”).

noun:Branntwein.tx: From late Middle High German brantwīn, contraction of older gebranter wīn, which latter is equivalent to modern gebrannter Wein (“distilled wine”, literally “burnt wine”).

noun:Bitterkeit.tx: From Middle High German bitterkeit, from Old High German bittarīgheit. Analysable as bitter + -keit.

verb:behelfen.tx: From Middle High German behëlfen, equivalent to be- + helfen. Compare Middle Low German behelpen, English behelp.

adj:belämmert.tx: Past participle of the rarer verb belämmern or belemmern (“to annoy", "to molest”), from Middle Low German belemmeren. The verb pertains to lahm (“lame”) and is cognate with Dutch belemmeren (“to hamper”). The semantic development of the adjective in German is, at least in part, due to association with Lamm (“lamb”, plural Lämmer), a supposedly naïve or stupid animal. Hence also the …

verb:brausen.tx: From Middle High German brūsen, from Old High German *brūsen, from Proto-Germanic *brausijaną (“to break; crack; crackle”). More at bruise. The sense "to shower" is a back-formation from noun Brause, in turn from the "to make dissonant noise" sense of this verb.

verb:bedrücken.tx: From Middle High German bedrücken, from Old High German bidrukken, from Proto-West Germanic *biþrukkijan. Equivalent to be- + drücken. Doublet of bedrucken.

noun:Bregen.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German brēgen, from Old Saxon *bregin, *bragan, from Proto-West Germanic *bragn, from Proto-Germanic *bragną. Cognate with Old English bræġn / bræġen, Dutch brein, English brain.

verb:baggern.tx: From Dutch baggeren, which pertains to bagger (“mud”). The noun Bagger (“excavator”) is a German derivative.

noun:Bake.tx: 17th century, from Middle Low German bāke, from Old Frisian bāken, from Proto-West Germanic *baukn, from Proto-Germanic *baukną. Cognate with Dutch baak, English beacon.

verb:ballern.tx: From Late Middle High German bollern, from Middle Low German balderen, (with Low German -ld- → -ll-). Compare Dutch bolderen and bulderen. However, independent onomatopoeia is equally possible. The football sense via “to shoot” and through secondary association with Ball (“ball”). See also Bollerwagen.

adj:barsch.tx: Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German barsch (“sharp, pointed, strict (in taste)”), from Old Saxon *barsk, from Proto-Germanic *barskaz, from *barsaz (“bass, perch”).

noun:Beitel.tx: Via German Low German from Middle Low German beitel. High German equivalents (beißel, etc.) are attested a couple of times. Cognate with Dutch beitel.

verb:beschwichtigen.tx: Via German Low German from Middle Low German beswichtigen. Pertaining to Dutch zwichten and Old High German giswiftēn with the Low German (and Dutch) development -ft- → -cht- (compare Nichte). Ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *swībaną.

noun:Bodden.tx: Via Low German and Middle Low German bodden (alongside bodem and other variants), from Old Saxon bodom. Doublet of Boden.

noun:Böschung.tx: From a western, probably Alemannic German, form of Busch (“bush”) – compare Luxembourgish Bësch – directly suffixed with -ung. The expected underlying verb böschen is only attested later and probably a back-formation.

noun:Böttcher.tx: In its modern form pertaining to Bottich (“tub”), but not directly related to it. Instead from Middle Low German bödeker with the Low German suffix -ker from böde (“barrel”) (compare Bütt); in early modern German (East Central German) adapted to the High German consonantism as botticher (at that time possibly already associated with Bottich).

noun:Brasse.tx: A Central and Low German form with -ss- for -chs-, from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German brassem, from Old High German brahsma, from Proto-West Germanic *brahsima, from Proto-Germanic *brahsmǭ, perhaps from *brehwanaz (“shining, glittery, sparkly”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerek- (“to shine”), see also English braid (verb). The form has widely replaced the more southern …

noun:Brackwasser.tx: Borrowed from Dutch brakwater, from Middle Dutch brak (“salty”). Compare brackig (which seems to be of Low German origin, although it could also be Dutch).

adj:brackig.tx: Via German Low German from Middle Low German brak (“salty”). Compare Brackwasser (from Dutch).

noun:Buddel.tx: From German Low German Buddel, which is borrowed from French bouteille with softening of stem-internal stops as found in some dialects of Low German (including that of Hamburg).

verb:buddeln.tx: 18th century. Variant of a Low German and Central German verb (pudeln, puddeln); see pudeln (“to splash, dabble”). The contemporary form seems to have spread from Berlin.

verb:bugsieren.tx: Borrowed from Dutch boegseren, from Portuguese puxar with influence of boeg (the cognate of German Bug (“bow of a ship”)), from Latin pulsare. Doublet of pulsieren.

verb:bollern.tx: From late Middle High German, related to boln, Böller (“firecracker”), or instead borrowed from German Low German. All eventually of onomatopoeic origin.

noun:Buxe.tx: Via Middle Low German buxe (seemingly from *bock-hose; see Hose). Also a West Central German word; compare Ripuarian Botz, Luxembourgish Box.

noun:Buchecker.tx: Compound of Buche + Ecker. The now rare simplex Ecker from Middle High German ackeran, eckern; only once attested in Old High German ekarn. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *akraną, whence also English acorn. An original neuter or masculine whose final -n was interpreted as a plural morpheme and which was subsequently made into a feminine. Kluge (24th edition) considers it a chiefly Low German word …

noun:Briefkastenfirma.tx: From Briefkasten (“mailbox”) + Firma (“company”), from the notion that it is merely a name and an address.

noun:Brod.tx: See the main entry. The -d may be from Low German and West Central German influence, but may also be a mainly graphic development due to the relatively rare occurrence of inflected forms (interchangeable Brot ~ Brodt ~ Brod and then by analogy also Brodes etc.).

adj:barmherzig.tx: Inherited from Middle High German barmherze(c), from Old High German armherz, a calque of Latin misericors. By surface analysis, barmen + Herz + -ig (for the first element see Erbarmen). Cognate with Gothic 𐌰𐍂𐌼𐌰𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍂𐍄𐍃 (armahairts), Old English earmheort.

noun:Bruttoinlandsprodukt.tx: brutto (“gross”) + Inlandsprodukt (“domestic product”), the latter from Inland (“homeland”) + Produkt (“product”).

noun:Blatter.tx: With sporadic shortening before -ter (as in Mutter) from Middle High German blātere, from Old High German blātara, from Proto-West Germanic *blādrā. Cognate with Dutch blaar, English bladder.

verb:belügen.tx: From Middle High German beliegen, from Old High German biliogan, from Proto-West Germanic *bileugan. Equivalent to be- + lügen.

verb:bedecken.tx: From Middle High German bedecken, from Old High German bidecken, bidekken, bithecken, from Proto-West Germanic *biþakkjan, equivalent to be- + decken.

noun:Bimbo.tx: Uncertain. The proper noun already occurs in the 19th century, and already as a name for a black person.

noun:Barde.tx: Borrowed from French barde, from Latin bardus.

noun:Brat.tx: From Middle High German gebræte, from Old High German brāto.

noun:Brät.tx: From Middle High German gebræte, from Old High German brāto, cognate with English brawn.

noun:Bärin.tx: From Middle High German birin, from Old High German berin. By surface analysis, Bär + -in.

verb:baumeln.tx: 17th century, exact etymology is uncertain. Perhaps from Baum (“tree”) + -eln (frequentative) as in “dangle from a tree”, but more likely an East Central German byform of bammeln, bummeln (both originally “to dangle”).

verb:bimmeln.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German bimmeln, of onomatopoeic origin.

noun:Batik.tx: Borrowed from Dutch batik, from Javanese bathik.

noun:Bosheit.tx: From Middle High German bōsheit, from Old High German bōsheit. By surface analysis, böse (“evil, malicious, wicked”) + -heit (“-ness”).

phrase:beim Barte des Propheten.tx: Literally, “by the beard of the prophet”; documented since the 18th century. There are two different etymological interpretations: * The (pre-)Islamic custom of touching the beard while taking a vow is well known from many oriental stories. verb:bestatten.tx: From Middle High German bestaten, from Old High German bistaten, since the 11th century. Related to Old High German stat, whence German Statt, Stadt, Stätte.

noun:Blindschleiche.tx: From Middle High German blintslīche, corresponding to blind + Schleicher, from schleichen (“to sneak; to slither”).

noun:Bierwurst.tx: Bier + Wurst, as intended to be served with beer.

adj:burlesk.tx: Borrowed from French burlesque, from Italian burlesco.

noun:Brennpunkt.tx: Calque of New Latin pūnctum ūstiōnis (17th c.), after the fact that sun rays burn when concentrated in a focus. By surface analysis, brennen + Punkt

adj:begehrlich.tx: From Late Middle High German begerlich; Begehr + -lich.

noun:Buhne.tx: From Middle Low German būne (“groyne, breakwater”). Possibly related to Bühne.

noun:Bammel.tx: Deverbal of regional bammeln (“to dangle”) (compare standard baumeln), referencing the uncertainty that comes with fear.

phrase:bestes Wissen und Gewissen.tx: Literally, “(one's) best knowledge and conscience”. Compare Dutch best weten en geweten.

noun:Back.tx: From Middle Low German bak (“bowl, box, chest”), from Middle Dutch bak (modern Dutch bak), from Old French bac (“large bowl”). Related with Becken, but unrelated with Backbord. The sense “dining table” is due to the fact that several sailors would eat from one bowl, so the word Back came to be used for the entire area that they shared. The sense “forecastle” might be a further generalisation …

noun:Bärendienst.tx: From Bär (“bear”) + -en- + Dienst (“service”). Compare Swedish björntjänst, Danish bjørnetjeneste, Norwegian Nynorsk bjørneteneste, Russian медвежья услуга (medvežʹja usluga) and similar forms in other languages. From the French fable L’Ours et l’Amateur des jardins by Jean de La Fontaine, in which a tame bear wants to do his master a favour by hitting a fly that has sat down on the master's …

verb:befruchten.tx: 16th century, from be- + Frucht + -en, perhaps an alteration of Middle High German bevrühtigen (“to sow a field”).

verb:begießen.tx: From Middle High German begieȥen, from Old High German bigioȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *bigeutan. Equivalent to be- + gießen.

noun:Brevier.tx: From late Middle High German breviere, from Latin breviarium.

adv:bäuchlings.tx: From Bauch + -lings; compare Middle High German biuchelingen, būchelingen.

noun:Bienenstich.tx: Biene (“bee”) + Stich (“sting”). Its origin is unclear. Various theories have been proposed. The most common theories are: * Stich could also mean "stocked up mass". verb:beiwohnen.tx: From Middle High German bīwonen; analyzable as bei + wohnen. At least in part, probably a calque of Latin cohabitāre.

verb:belachen.tx: From Middle High German belachen, from Old High German *bihlahhan, from Proto-West Germanic *bihlahhjan. Equivalent to be- + lachen.

noun:Bussi.tx: Probably of imitative origin and related to Central Franconian Butz (“kiss”).

noun:Beduine.tx: Borrowed from French Bédouin, from Arabic بَدَوِيِّين (badawiyyīn), colloquial plural of بَدَوِيّ (badawiyy), from بَدْو (badw, “desert, camp”).

verb:berauben.tx: From Middle High German berouben, from Old High German biroubon, from Proto-Germanic *biraubōną; equivalent to be- + rauben. Cognate with Dutch beroven, English bereave, Danish berøve, Norwegian berøve, Swedish beröva.

verb:brodeln.tx: From late Old High German brodeln.

verb:bibbern.tx: The contemporary form since the 19th century from Low German bibbern, probably already Middle Low German *bibberen, a frequentative of bēven (from Old Saxon bibōn, bivon), from Proto-West Germanic *bibēn, cognate of modern German beben. Compare Dutch bibberen (1700), English biver. In spite of the late attestations, these informal verbs might be rather old in view of the etymologically regular …

verb:befreunden.tx: From Middle High German vriunden. By surface analysis, be- + Freund + -en. Cognate with English befriend.

noun:Bitter.tx: From Middle High German bitter, bittære, biter, bitære, equivalent to bitten + -er. Compare Middle Low German biddære, Saterland Frisian Bidder, English bidder.

adj:befahren.tx: From the null-morphological past participle of the above verb.

verb:befangen.tx: From Middle High German bevāhen, from Old High German bifāhan, from Proto-West Germanic *bifą̄han. Equivalent to be- + fangen. The homonymic past participle is continued as adjective.

adj:befangen.tx: From Middle High German bevangen, from Old High German bifangan, from Proto-West Germanic *bifangan. Synchronically, the past participle of etymology 1.

adj:beflissen.tx: Past participle of now possibly obsolete befleißen (“to endeavour, to attempt”).

adj:behände.tx: From Middle High German behende (“suitably, conveniently, skilfully, quickly”), univerbation of Old High German bī henti (literally “at hand”).

adj:beinhart.tx: From Bein + hart (“hard”), the former word being used in the (now dated) sense “bone”.

adj:bejahrt.tx: From Middle High German bejāret, equivalent to be- + Jahr (“year”) + -t. Compare Dutch bejaard, Saterland Frisian bejierd.

adj:beschaulich.tx: From Middle High German beschouwelich; equivalent to beschauen + -lich.

adj:bibelfest.tx: From Bibel + fest. Cf. Dutch Bijbelvast.

adj:bissig.tx: From Middle High German bīȥic, bīȥec, *biȥȥic, from Old High German biȥȥīg, bīȥīg, equivalent to Biss + -ig. Doublet of beißig. Cognate with Middle Low German bētich.

adj:bucklig.tx: Buckel + -ig. Compare Middle High German buckeleht.

noun:Brink.tx: Borrowed from Low German Brink, from Middle Low German brink, from Proto-Germanic *brinkaz. Cognate with Dutch brink, English brink.

noun:Burmeister.tx: Said to come from Low German roots cognate with Bauer + Meister. Compare Bürgermeister.

noun:Brain.tx: Borrowed from English brain. Doublet of Bregen.

noun:Buchmacher.tx: From Middle High German buochmachære, from Old High German buohmahhāri, buohmahheri. Equivalent to Buch + Macher. The sense “bookie” (19th c.) is a semantic loan from English bookmaker.

noun:Brückenkopf.tx: 18th century, a calque of French tête de pont.

noun:Blütezeit.tx: From Blüte (“blossom”) + Zeit (“time”). Compare Dutch bloeitijd.

verb:bedrängen.tx: From a merger of: * Middle High German bedrangen, bedrengen (both also attested in Early New High German), both from Old High German bidrangōn, from Proto-West Germanic *biþrangōn; and * Middle High German bedringen (also attested in Early New High German), from Old High German bidringan, from Proto-West Germanic *biþringwan. All forms ultimatively from Proto-Indo-European *trenkʷ- (“to beat, …

verb:betäuben.tx: From Middle High German betöuben, betouben, from be- + töuben (“to deafen”), the latter from Old High German touben, from Proto-West Germanic *daubijan. Cognate with Dutch doven. By surface analysis, be- + taub (“deaf, numb”) + -en; compare ein tauber Zeh (“a numb toe”).

noun:Bilirubin.tx: From New Latin, from Latin bīlis (“bile”) + ruber or rubeus (“red”) + -in. The German word was naturalized into other languages as international scientific vocabulary (e.g., bilirubin, bilirubine, bilirubina).

noun:Bankert.tx: From Middle High German banchart. Compare Bavarian Bånkert.

noun:Buschmann.tx: From Busch + Mann, a calque of Dutch Bosjesman.

verb:beschmieren.tx: From Middle High German besmirwen, from Old High German bismirwen, from Proto-West Germanic *bismirwijan. By surface analysis, be- + schmieren. Cognate with Dutch besmeren and English besmear.

noun:Bafög.tx: Abbreviation of Bundesausbildungsförderungsgesetz (“Federal Training Assistance Act”).

noun:Brunft.tx: From Middle High German brunft, from Old High German brumft, from Proto-Germanic *brumþiz.

noun:Baronesse.tx: Derived from Baron in relation to French baronne.

noun:Beinstellen.tx: Nominalisation of ein Bein stellen. Equivalent to Bein + Stellen.

noun:Bazi.tx: Probably a shortening of Lumpazi or Lumpazius.

noun:Botulismus.tx: Pseudo-Latinism, coined from Latin botulus (“sausage”) with the addition of the Latinate suffix -ismus.

phrase:Befehl ist Befehl.tx: Literally, “order is order”. Used as a defence during the Nuremberg trials (see Nuremberg defense).

verb:blähen.tx: From Middle High German blæjen, from Old High German blāen, from Proto-West Germanic *blāan, from Proto-Germanic *blēaną. Cognate with obsolete Dutch blaaien, English blow.

verb:besaufen.tx: From Middle High German besūfen. Equivalent to be- + saufen.

noun:Bullauge.tx: Partial calque of English bullseye, in its now-obsolete nautical meaning.

verb:bestreichen.tx: From Middle High German bestrīchen, from Old High German bistrīhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *bistrīkan. Equivalent to be- + streichen. Cognate with Dutch bestrijken.

noun:Beischlaf.tx: Deverbal from beischlafen. Compare Yiddish בײַשלאָף (bayshlof), Alemannic German Bischlof, Dutch bijslaap.

verb:belehren.tx: From Middle High German *belēren, from Old High German bilēren. Equivalent to be- + lehren.

verb:bebauen.tx: From Middle High German bebūwen, from Old High German bibūan, bibūwan, bibūen, bibūwen. Equivalent to be- + bauen.

verb:buttern.tx: From Late Middle High German *buttern, puttern (15th c.). By surface analysis, Butter + -n.

noun:Biet.tx: Inherited from Middle High German biet.

noun:Balz.tx: From Middle High German balz, also balzer (“courtship, mop of hair, ponytail”), attested from the 14th century onwards. Compare Middle High German balzieren (“to tie one's hair into a ponytail”). Further etymology unknown. Possibly linked to Proto-Germanic *baltijaz.

verb:bestürzen.tx: From Middle High German bestürzen, from Old High German bisturzen. Equivalent to be- + stürzen.

noun:Berührungsangst.tx: Berührung + -s- + Angst. Compare Dutch beroeringsangst and Danish berøringsangst.

noun:Bürgschaft.tx: From Middle High German bürgeschaft, from Old High German burgiscaf. By surface analysis, Bürge (“guarantor”) + -schaft (“-ship”).

verb:beweinen.tx: From Middle High German beweinen, from Old High German biweinōn, from Proto-West Germanic *biwainōn. Equivalent to be- + weinen. Cognate with Dutch bewenen.

noun:Besatz.tx: Back-formation from besetzen (“to occupy; to staff, to cast; to edge, to trim, to line”).

noun:Bordüre.tx: 17th century, borrowed from French bordure, ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic *burdą.

noun:Borte.tx: From Middle High German borte, from Old High German borto.

verb:blaumachen.tx: From blau + machen. The semantic motivation is unclear. Perhaps compare blauer Montag (“holiday Monday”, literally “blue Monday”).

noun:Begehr.tx: From Late Middle High German begër f; see Gier for more.

verb:behelligen.tx: From be- + helligen (“to plague”), from hellig (“tired, exhausted”).

noun:Ballermann.tx: From colloquial ballern (“to bang, to shoot”) and Mann (“man”).

noun:Beinwell.tx: From Middle High German beinwelle, from Old High German beinwella, beinwalla.

verb:bewerfen.tx: From Middle High German bewërfen, from Old High German biwërfan, from Proto-West Germanic *biwerpan. Equivalent to be- + werfen. Cognate with Dutch bewerpen.

verb:brocken.tx: From Middle High German brocken, from Old High German brocchōn, from Proto-West Germanic *brekan.

noun:Batzen.tx: From dialectal batzen (“to be sticky, soft; to stick together”), from backen (“to stick together, cake”), because of the appearance of the coins.

verb:bewenden.tx: From Middle High German bewenden, from Old High German biwenten, from Proto-West Germanic *biwandijan, from Proto-Germanic *biwandijaną (“to turn around”), equivalent to be- + wenden. Cognate with English bewend.

verb:bäumen.tx: From Middle High German boumen. Equivalent to Baum (“a tree”) + -en referring to the way trees grow up high.

noun:Bohei.tx: From Low German (e.g. Westphalian, East Frisian) and Central Franconian dialects. First attested as Dutch bohay in 1573 (now in the form poeha). Possibly of common origin with French brouhaha, be this onomatopoeic or from Hebrew בָּרוּךְ הַבָּא (bārûḵ hab-bā, literally “blessed be he who comes”); see the French for more. Alternatively the Dutch/German form may be an independent onomatopoeia.

noun:Bluthund.tx: From the 15th century, from Blut (“blood”) + Hund (“dog, hound”). Compare Dutch bloedhond, Low German Bloothund, English bloodhound, Common Scandinavian blodhund.

noun:Burgfrieden.tx: From Middle High German burcvriede (“special legal status of a castle shared by several heirs, strictly forbidding violence like feuds etc. within”). Can be analysed synchronously as Burg (“castle, fortification”) + Frieden (“peace”). Revived by national romanticism in the 19th century and applied especially to the suspension of inter-party rivalry in the German Empire during World War I.

verb:besehen.tx: From Middle High German besehen, from Old High German bisehan, from Proto-West Germanic *bisehwan, from Proto-Germanic *bisehwaną. Equivalent to be- + sehen.

noun:Bedacht.tx: From Middle High German bedāht(e) f (12th c.), deverbal from bedenken.

verb:betören.tx: From Middle High German betœren. By surface analysis, be- + Tor (“fool”) + -en.

verb:besagen.tx: From Middle High German besagen, from Old High German bisagēn, from Proto-West Germanic *bisaggjan. By surface analysis, be- + sagen. Cognate with English besay.

verb:buhlen.tx: From Middle High German buolen (“to woo, love”), from buole (“friend, lover, loved one”). Cognate with Middle Low German bôlen (“to woo, court”). Compare Dutch boelen.

noun:Blockhaus.tx: Calque of English blockhouse (early 19th century) and from (Holz-)Block (“(wooden) block”) + Haus (“house”).

noun:Bakelit.tx: Patented July 1907 by its inventor, Leo Hendrik Baekeland. See -it.

noun:Bocher.tx: The word was borrowed via Yiddish בחור (bokher) which in Western Yiddish applied the senses of “boy, youngster, man”, “Talmud student”, especially “Talmud student who gave lessons to Jewish children in exchange for board and lodge”, “teacher of religious education”, “Jewish teacher”, “assistant schoolmaster”, from Hebrew בָּחוּר (bakhúr, “young man”). Sense 2 is attested since the 18th century. …

noun:Bodenfrost.tx: From Boden (“ground, soil”) + Frost (“frost, freezing weather”).

noun:Blumenverkäuferin.tx: From Blume (“flower”) + -n- + Verkäuferin (“female seller”), or rather from Blumenverkäufer (“flower seller”) + -in (“female”).

verb:bagatellisieren.tx: From Bagatelle + -isieren. The verb is attested since the early 20th century and a derivative of Bagatelle.

noun:Bodega.tx: Borrowed from Spanish bodega. Doublet of Apotheke and Boutique.

noun:Blähsucht.tx: From blähen (“to cause flatulation”) + Sucht (“anxiety; sickness; addiction”).

noun:Beuge.tx: From Middle High German biuge, from Old High German piugo, deverbal of piugan. Equivalent to beug- + -e.

noun:Bohemien.tx: Borrowed from French bohémien, eventually from etymology 2 below.

noun:Brimborium.tx: Borrowed from French brimborion, from Ecclesiastical Latin breviārium (“breviary”).

verb:bestäuben.tx: From be- + stäuben or Staub + be- -en.

verb:bezuschussen.tx: be- + Zuschuss + -en. First attested in the first half of the 20th century.

verb:bezeigen.tx: be- + zeigen. Compare obsolete English beteach.

verb:begatten.tx: From Middle High German begaten (“to reach, meet, join”), from Old High German bigatōn. Equivalent to be- + Gatte (“spouse”, originally “companion”) + -en. The modern sense of the verb (17th c.) follows the semantic development of the noun. Not related with English beget.

verb:blechen.tx: From Rotwelsch Blech (“money”) + -en. Originally student slang.

verb:balsamieren.tx: From Middle High German balsemen, balsmen. By surface analysis, Balsam + -ieren.

noun:Biker.tx: Borrowed from English biker, in the cycling sense perhaps a clipping of Mountainbiker, from Mountainbike.

noun:Blaumann.tx: From blau (“blue”) + Mann (“man”). Compare French bleu de travail.

noun:Bramsegel.tx: Unclear, see Dutch bramzeil for more.

noun:Bergfried.tx: From Middle High German bërcvrit, bërvrit, bërvride. Further etymology unknown. A common folk etymology is the derivation from bergen (“to protect”) and Frieden (“peace”). Cognate with English belfry.

noun:Bouteille.tx: Borrowed from French bouteille. Doublet of Buddel.

noun:Blumenkind.tx: Blume + -n- + Kind, calque of English flower child.

noun:Bodybag.tx: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from body + bag. The English term body bag refers to a bag designed to contain a human corpse; the German term for that is Leichensack.

noun:Bitternis.tx: bitter + -nis. Compare Middle High German biternisse (Central German, 1338).

noun:Bierhaus.tx: From Middle High German bierhūs, from Old High German *biorhūs, from Proto-West Germanic *beuʀahūs, equivalent to Bier + Haus.

noun:Bre.tx: Likely from the Serbo-Croatian interjection or adverb bre; compare also Swedish bre for this.

noun:Borretsch.tx: From Middle High German boretsch, buretsch, which reflects a Romance language pronunciation of Medieval Latin borāgō. Compare French bourrache.

noun:Bambule.tx: Borrowed from French bamboula, originally prison slang.

verb:beizen.tx: From Middle High German beiʒen, from Old High German beizen, from Proto-West Germanic *baitijan. Etymologically, a causative of beißen.

noun:Bede.tx: From northern Middle High German bede and Middle Low German bēde, from Proto-Germanic *bedō (“plea”). Doublet of Bitte (“plea”). The use for a tax developed in Middle High German.

adv:beieinander.tx: From Middle High German bīeinander. Equivalent to bei- + einander.

noun:Büttner.tx: From Middle High German büt(t)enære. By surface analysis, Bütte + -ner.

noun:Blesse.tx: Middle High German blasse, Old High German blassa, from Proto-West Germanic *blasī, from Proto-Germanic *blasį̄. Cognate with Dutch bles.

noun:Bärchen.tx: From Bär + -chen. Equivalent to Old Norse Bjarki.

noun:Bummelant.tx: From the 19th century, from Studentensprache, bummeln + -ant.

noun:Bille.tx: First mentioned in 1075 as Bilena. According to Albrecht Greule, of native Germanic origin and from some derivation of Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“white, bright”). Or, from a Slavic derivation of the same root, similar to the river Biela.

noun:Bräu.tx: From Middle High German briuwe (“brewing”, noun).

verb:beflecken.tx: From Middle High German bevlecken, from Old High German gifleckōn. By surface analysis, be- + Fleck + -en.

verb:befleißigen.tx: From be- + Fleiß + -igen. Cognate with Dutch bevlijtigen.

verb:beuteln.tx: From Middle High German biuteln. By surface analysis, Beutel + -n.

noun:Beutelschneider.tx: From Middle High German biutelsnīder. Equivalent to Beutel (“pouch”) + schneiden (“to cut”) + -er (“-er”) or Beutel + Schneider. Maybe a calque of Latin crumēniseca.

verb:brunzen.tx: From Middle High German brunzen, brunnezen, intensive of brunnen, derived from Middle High German brunne (“well (noun)”). See also Bavarian brunzn.

noun:Brünne.tx: Inherited from Old High German brunja, from Proto-West Germanic *brunnjā. Cognate with Old English byrne.

noun:Buhurt.tx: From Middle High German būhurt, bēhurt, or Middle Low German bohurt, burt, later the term for a ”tournament-melee”, a medieval tournament game, in which mock combat is conducted between two groups of knights, alternatively a game in which an attack was made on a pretend fortress, but also a synonym for tournament in general. Cognates includes Old Italian bohordicum; English bohort; French bohourt …

noun:Bundeshymne.tx: From Bund (“federation”) + -es- + Hymne (“anthem”). Shortening of Österreichische Bundeshymne.

verb:besiedeln.tx: From Middle High German besidelen. In the modern sense only since the 19th century. By surface analysis, be- + siedeln.

noun:Betel.tx: Borrowed from Portuguese bétele, from Malayalam വെറ്റില (veṟṟila).

noun:Benachteiligter.tx: From benachteiligt, past participle of benachteiligen.

verb:bunkern.tx: From Bunker (“bunker, place for storing coal”) + -n.

adj:begreiflich.tx: Middle High German begrīflich, by surface analysis, begreifen + -lich.

verb:bemessen.tx: From Middle High German *bemëȥȥen, from Old High German bimëȥȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *bimetan. Equivalent to be- + messen. Cognate with Dutch bemeten and obsolete English bemete.

noun:Blödheit.tx: From Middle High German blœdecheit, blœdekeit. By surface analysis, blöd + -heit.

noun:Baude.tx: Attested 15th century, standard since 19th century. From Silesian East Central German, from Czech bouda, from Old Czech búda, buda, from Middle High German buode, whence also inherited Bude.

noun:Bleichgesicht.tx: Calque of English paleface. Equivalent to bleich + Gesicht.

noun:Bestenliste.tx: Beste (“best [things, people]”, nominalization) + -n- + Liste, literally “list of the best”.

noun:Babo.tx: Borrowed from a Southeast European or West Asian language, possibly borrowed multiple times from several languages in different German subcultures. The word was popularised by rapper Haftbefehl (who is of Turkish and Zaza ancestry) in his 2012 single "Chabos wissen wer der Babo ist" ("Boys know who the boss is"), and the most likely derivation is from Zazaki babo (“father”), possibly influenced …

noun:Berufsunfähigkeit.tx: From berufsunfähig (“unfit for work”) + -keit; equivalent to Beruf (“occupation”) + -s- + Unfähigkeit (“inability”).

noun:Bluterkrankheit.tx: From Bluter (“haemophiliac, bleeder”) + Krankheit (“illness, disease”). Compare English bleeding sickness.

noun:Betriebsferien.tx: From Betrieb (“operation, business, company”) + -s- + Ferien (“break, holiday”).

verb:besiegeln.tx: From Middle High German besigelen, from Old High German bisigilen, from Proto-West Germanic *bisiglijan, from Latin sigillō (“to seal”). Equivalent to be- + siegeln.

noun:Beriberi.tx: Late 17th century, from Dutch berebery (1612), beriberij (1631), possibly through French béribéri (1665). The Dutch is either from Portuguese berebere (1568) or directly from a language of Southeast Asia. The ultimate origin is usually identified as Sinhalese බැරි (bæri, “weakness, incapacity”). An older theory connects it with Malay biri-biri (“sheep”, a supposedly dull and weak animal).

verb:besingen.tx: From Middle High German besingen, from Old High German bisingan, from Proto-West Germanic *bisingwan, equivalent to be- + singen. Cognate with Middle Low German besingen, Dutch bezingen, English besing.

noun:Bra.tx: Clipping of Bratan, itself a borrowing from Russian брата́н (bratán). Compare also English bra.

noun:Bries.tx: From Middle High German briz (14th c.). This late and singular attestation allows no certainty about the quality of the vowel or the final alveolar. Origin unknown. Possibly related with Proto-Germanic *breustą (“breast”) or *breutaną (“to crush”). Compare also English brisket, whose -k- does not fit with the German form, however. Danish brissel, Swedish bräss (“thymus”) are probably from German.

noun:Brennball.tx: From brennen (“to burn”) + Ball (“ball”), possibly because the players who are "out" are said to be verbrannt (“burnt”).

verb:behängen.tx: From Middle High German behāhen. Equivalent to be- + hängen.

noun:Birkenstocks.tx: From the name of the company, Birkenstock.

noun:Barett.tx: 15th century, from Middle French barrete and Italian barretta, barretto.

noun:Bahnwärter.tx: From Bahn (“rail, railway, railroad”) + Wärter (“attendant, keeper, guard, warder”).

noun:Brass.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German bras (“din, racket”), related to prassen.

noun:Barkasse.tx: Borrowed from French barcasse, from Italian barcaccia.

noun:Begünstigter.tx: From begünstigt (“fostered, abetted, benefited”) + -er; a substantivization of begünstigt, past participle of begünstigen.

phrase:bitte, das Spiel zu machen.tx: Calque of French faites vos jeux. Literally, “[I] ask [you] to make the play”, or more loosely translated as “please make your play”.

verb:beisitzen.tx: From Middle High German bīsitzen. Equivalent to bei- + sitzen.

noun:Blide.tx: From Middle High German blīde, from Medieval Latin blida. The undiphthongised form may be of dialectal origin, but was probably reinforced by learned influence.

noun:Blindenschrift.tx: By surface analysis, Blinden (genitive of Blinder, a substantivized adjective from blind) + Schrift (“script, writing”).

verb:beuten.tx: From Middle High German biuten (“to treat something as booty”), borrowed from Middle Low German bûten (“to plunder”). By surface analysis, Beute (“booty”) + -n.

noun:Begabter.tx: Nominalisation of the adjective begabt (“talented, gifted”).

noun:Berittener.tx: Nominalisation of the adjective beritten (“mounted, on horseback”).

verb:befüllen.tx: From Middle High German *bevüllen, from Old High German bifullen. Equivalent to be- + füllen.

verb:befühlen.tx: From Middle High German bevüelen, from Old High German bifuolōn, bifolōn. Equivalent to be- + fühlen.

verb:beisein.tx: From Middle High German bīsīn, from Old High German bīsīn. Obsolete since Early New High German, but is continued as deverbalised noun.

verb:bescheinen.tx: From Middle High German beschīnen, from Old High German biskīnan, from Proto-West Germanic *biskīnan, from Proto-Germanic *biskīnaną. Equivalent to be- + scheinen. Cognates include Dutch beschijnen, English beshine and Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐍃𐌺𐌴𐌹𐌽𐌰𐌽 (biskeinan).

verb:beschauen.tx: From Middle High German beschouwen, from Old High German biskouwōn, from Proto-West Germanic *biskauwōn. Equivalent to be- + schauen. Cognate with Dutch beschouwen and Old English besceawian.

verb:bestecken.tx: From Middle High German bestecken, from Old High German bistekken. By surface analysis, be- + stecken.

verb:beträufeln.tx: beträufen + -eln, iterative of beträufen, from older betraufen, from Middle High German betroufen, from Old High German bitroufen.

noun:Brühl.tx: Probably from Gaulish *brogilos, from Proto-Celtic *mrogis. See that entry and bröol for more.

noun:Blindkopie.tx: From blind + Kopie, probably a calque of English blind copy.

noun:Bemme.tx: A West Slavic borrowing, synonymous to Upper Sorbian pomazka, Lower Sorbian pomazka, Masovian Polish pomazanka.

adj:buckelig.tx: Buckel + -ig. Compare Middle High German buckeleht.

noun:Bodenfreiheit.tx: From Boden + Freiheit. Compare Dutch bodemvrijheid.

noun:Bahnhofsmission.tx: From Bahnhof (“train station”) + -s- + Mission (“mission, missionary service”).

noun:Bälde.tx: 17th century, equivalent to bald (“soon”) + -e (“-ness”). Possibly continues Middle High German belde, from Old High German beldī, but these are only attested in the sense “audacity”, belonging to the related Middle High German adjective balt (“audacious, bold”), which was lost by the 15th century. Therefore an independent coinage is more likely.

noun:Blutdurst.tx: Blut (“blood”) + Durst (“thirst”) Compare Dutch bloeddorst and English bloodthirst.

noun:Blutspur.tx: Blut + Spur. Compare Dutch bloedspoor and Swedish blodspår.

noun:Beckmesser.tx: Figurative sense after the character Sixtus Beckmesser in Richard Wagner's opera Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg (1867).

noun:Bewusstseinsstrom.tx: From Bewusstsein + -s- + Strom. Calque of English stream of consciousness.

adj:bienenfleißig.tx: Biene + -n- + fleißig, literally “busy as a bee”.

noun:Betriebswirt.tx: Back-formation from Betriebswirtschaft. By surface analysis, Betrieb + -s- + Wirt.

noun:Butterfahrt.tx: From Butter (“butter”) + Fahrt (“trip”), from butter being a common item offered on these trips in the 1950s and 1960s.

noun:Brausetablette.tx: From brausen (“to roar, to whoosh”) + Tablette (“tablet”).

noun:Bestandsverzeichnis.tx: Bestand (“stock; inventory; assets”) + Verzeichnis (“directory; list; index”)

noun:Besing.tx: Diminutive formation of German Low German bes (“berry”).

noun:Bauunternehmer.tx: From Bau + Unternehmer or bauen + Unternehmer.

noun:Basejumper.tx: Borrowed from English BASE jumper, from BASE (“building, antenna, span, earth”) + jumper.

adv:bisserl.tx: Adverbialized noun Bisserl, from Bissen (“a bit, bite”) + -erl (diminutive suffix).

verb:beleiben.tx: From Middle High German blīben, belīben (“to remain in the same position, pause, blin”), from Old High German bilīban (“to remain”), from Proto-Germanic *bilībaną (“to remain”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick, glue”). Cognate with Dutch blijven (“to remain”), English belive (“to remain, stay”). More at belive.
